World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Disaster diplomacy and a persistent peso
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum spent the weekend before this week began in Puebla, kicking off the 2026 National Reforestation Day from the mountain pass between the Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl volcanoes. There, marking the International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples, she declared that the Paso de Cortés — named for the conquistador who marched through it in 1519 — would be a great candidate for a new name.

On Monday morning, the president’s attention had shifted south: a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, killing hundreds. Sheinbaum immediately pledged Mexico would send Colombia everything it needed, but the country’s military rescue brigade quickly ran into a diplomatic hurdle, part of a tangle of certification disputes and friction that unfolded even as quietly extraordinary Mexican solidarity continued — not just with Colombia, but with wildfire-stricken Canada as well. Colombia’s quake also revived an old question for Mexico, one we explore in more depth here: with Venezuela and now Colombia both rattled by major temblors this year, does Mexico’s own position on the Pacific Ring of Fire mean its odds just went up?

Otherwise, the week of Aug. 10-14 in Mexico brought big economic headlines, athletic glory and advances in the Ayotzinapa criminal case.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Mexico extends a hand abroad

Mexico’s instinct to help its neighbors was on full display this week. More than 300 Mexican firefighters traveled to British Columbia to help battle over 100 active wildfires that have forced tens of thousands to evacuate, drawing an outpouring of gratitude on Canadian social media. Farther south, a 45-member team of Mexico’s famed “Topos” rescue brigade reached Cali, Colombia, on Wednesday to dig through earthquake rubble — but only after Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella initially rejected their help, citing sovereignty concerns.

On Thursday, Sheinbaum confirmed that an official Mexican Army rescue brigade had not been authorized to enter Colombia and therefore remained at home. According to the president, Colombia’s new government demanded a type of certification the Mexican team does not have. Mexico kept sending humanitarian aid regardless — more than 58 tonnes of food, water and medicine by week’s end.

Ex-governor bound over in Ayotzinapa case

In one of the week’s most significant justice developments, former Guerrero Governor Ángel Aguirre was ordered to stand trial over his alleged role in the 2014 disappearance of 43 Ayotzinapa students. Prosecutors allege Aguirre ordered the destruction of security footage from Iguala’s Palace of Justice on the night the students vanished, partly to protect a nephew with ties to a local criminal gang. Aguirre, who resigned as governor weeks after the disappearances, remains jailed at the Altiplano maximum-security prison as the case — one of Mexico’s most notorious unsolved human rights tragedies — grinds toward trial nearly 12 years later.

The super peso returns

Mexico’s currency briefly broke back below 17 to the US dollar on Friday morning for the first time since 2024, in what analysts are calling the return of the “super peso.”

The peso has now strengthened for four consecutive days and appreciated more than 5% this year, a move Citibanamex attributes largely to global dollar weakness rather than Mexican fundamentals. Still, by the MND Peso Index™, which compares a basket of goods in Mexico and Dallas, the currency looks overvalued by 2.4% — a smaller gap than June’s 2.9%, suggesting the exchange rate isn’t too far removed from what prices on the ground would imply.

Homicides fall, but Sinaloa gets reinforcements

Security officials reported on Wednesday that the daily homicide average has fallen 51% since Sheinbaum took office, with July recording the lowest monthly tally of her administration so far. Even so, nearly half of the country’s murders remain concentrated in just seven states, Sinaloa among them. That reality was underscored by the Navy’s deployment of over 1,700 personnel to Mazatlán after the port city logged its bloodiest month of the year in July, as fighting between rival Sinaloa Cartel factions Los Chapitos and Los Mayos continues to spill beyond Culiacán into the tourist-heavy coastal city.

Visa fights spill into the mañanera

Washington’s campaign against Mexican political figures widened this week.

Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, the son of former President López Obrador and a former Morena party organization secretary, said the United States had revoked his visa, accusing Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his deputy of a politically motivated move. At Friday’s mañanera, Sheinbaum called the decision “essentially political in nature,” urging Washington to produce evidence against anyone it targets while insisting the dispute won’t spiral into a broader conflict with the United States.

Business indicators to know

Peso: Trading just above 17 to the dollar, its strongest level since February, even as the MND Peso Index™ pegs it as 2.4% overvalued.

Trading just above 17 to the dollar, its strongest level since February, even as the MND Peso Index™ pegs it as 2.4% overvalued. Inflation: July’s headline rate came in at 3.12%, its lowest since May 2020, though Banxico Governor Victoria Rodríguez says it’s too early to “claim victory.”

July’s headline rate came in at 3.12%, its lowest since May 2020, though Banxico Governor Victoria Rodríguez says it’s too early to “claim victory.” Jobs: Formal employment shed 19,550 positions in July, a seasonal dip IMSS attributes to the school year’s end, even as average wages hit a record daily high.

Formal employment shed 19,550 positions in July, a seasonal dip IMSS attributes to the school year’s end, even as average wages hit a record daily high. Industry: Industrial activity grew 0.2% month-on-month in June, lifted by mining and construction, while manufacturing logged its 12th straight month of annual decline.

Cyclospora cleared in the Riviera Maya

After British health authorities flagged a spike in cyclosporiasis cases among travelers returning from Mexico, Cofepris tested food and water samples from 16 Riviera Maya hotels — and found no trace of the parasite. All 43 samples, drawn from Playa del Carmen, Puerto Morelos, Tulum and Isla Mujeres, tested negative, and no contamination indicators turned up elsewhere. Mexico’s Health Ministry has confirmed 33 cyclosporiasis cases nationwide this year, a tiny fraction of the population, though the source of the UK cases remains unidentified.

Tourism notes

June brought 4.11 million international tourists to Mexico, up just 1.1% year-on-year — a muted bump given that Mexico hosted 12 of its 13 World Cup matches that month.

Tulum’s airport will regain five international routes this winter to cities in Canada and the United States, part of a state push to reverse a steep decline in international traffic.

Sargassum accumulation, though still tracking toward the second-heaviest year on record, has begun easing across most monitored stretches of the Quintana Roo coast as collection efforts and shifting currents bring relative relief to hard-hit beaches like Tulum and Playa del Carmen.

Mexican athletes seize the moment

It was a banner week for Mexican sport. The under-20 men’s soccer team defended its Concacaf title, beating the United States 2-0 at Mexico City’s Estadio Banorte for a record 15th championship, with defender Cristóbal Alfaro scoring twice.

Meanwhile, Mexico delivered its best-ever medal haul at the Central American and Caribbean Games, where the delegation topped the table with a record 407 medals in Santo Domingo. The government announced every medal — not just an athlete’s best result — will now earn a cash prize, a change Conade chief Rommel Pacheco said was Sheinbaum’s own idea.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: How fragile is Chacahua’s lagoon ecosystem? A conversation with locals on the Oaxaca coast
World.content:
A bus from Puerto Escondido. A minibus, aka colectivo, from Rio Grande. Then a lancha, or small boat, across the water to Zapotalito. One more open-air truck and you’ve made it.

Laguna de Chacahua sits along the western coast of Oaxaca, part of the state’s more than 300 milePacific coastline – a lagoon ecosystem padded with jungle flora, where the network of mangroves roots the island in its gurgling brackish tides.

It is part of the municipality of Villa de Tututepec de Melchor Ocampo and around 100 miles down the coast from the popular beach city of Puerto Escondido. In the daytime, the high sun smelts the soft sand and rocks while hammocks loll idly in the low breeze. After sunset, bioluminescent plankton set the water aglow in a neon blue glacé.

Technically, Chacahua is a barrier island, meaning it is not entirely separate from the mainland but is only accessible by boat. The community is predominantly Black and Afro-Indigenous, partially linking back to the Spanish enslavement of Africans and their forced labor in Mexico in the 16th and 17th centuries. But many residents make their way over from the mainland to surf, fish and enjoy the more relaxed pulse of daily life.

“Here, you can be whatever you want to be,” Augusto, an architect living in Chacahua, tells me. “And nobody is going to look down on you; you’re living in a free place.”

‘The sea is starting to reclaim the land’

But it isn’t all peace in paradise. Coastal environments and their communities are facing increased exposure to natural hazards.

The rainy season from June to September brings storms and natural climate variations, but Oaxaca state’s geography, situated along Mexico’s southwest Pacific coast, leaves it particularly vulnerable to climate change. Pacific hurricanes and Atlantic basin tropical systems pose a dual threat, alongside the increasing reality of heavy rains, droughts, and rising temperatures and sea levels.

While it is difficult to find more localised data for the island, average yearly temperature in Oaxaca City rose by 1.1 degrees Celsius (2 degrees Fahrenheit) between 1994 and 2024. While this figure may seem small, it represents a rapid change over three decades, even at the local level.

Global sea level rise has been affecting the coast of Oaxaca, and Chacahua is no exception. Drawing from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC) 6th Assessment Report, NASA’s Sea Level Projection projects extreme sea level rise along Oaxaca’s Pacific coast, and the lagoon’s low relief offers little defense.

Sitting in a cabana just 100 meters inland, Augusto points towards Playa Chacahua. “The sea is starting to reclaim (the) land. That’s why the houses over there are collapsing.”

It was Hurricane Pauline in 1997 that dramatically shifted the landscape of Chacahua, the lagoon rising to such a level that a new inlet was created and swathes of the beach were eaten away. Today, the beach faces an ever-greater risk due to the damaging erosion.

‘Everyone fishes sooner or later’

Fishing is integral to life in Chacahua, and the catch is diverse – shrimp, puffer fish, oysters, blue crabs, and red snapper by the Bajo Este. “There are all kinds of fish,” Antonio says. “There’s a bit of everything here.”

Antonio started fishing at the age of 8 with his grandfather. At 17, he began fishing for sharks; tiburoneros (shark fishermen) use a simbra, a 14-kilometre-long (9-mile) fishing line with around 300 hooks every 18 meters.

“We’d head out along the Guerrero coast, going out toward the horizon where the sun sets … to where you can’t see a thing anymore,” Antonio tells me. “Transatlantic ships pass through there. We’d stay one night and head back the next day.”

The population is no more than 800 and, according to Antonio, more than half of its residents are fishermen.

“Everyone fishes sooner or later,” he says. But security isn’t promised. “Later, some move onto other jobs because fishing is just a matter of luck.”

Santiago was born on the island and has been a fisherman for 20 years.

“Because of the rains and the storms that come, it’s more dangerous now. It’s more dangerous than compared to before. It used to be a good life.”

The ecocide of the Chacahua-Pastoría Lagoons is a key culprit, with toxic chemical influx from local oil-crop industries, as well as chemical waste from a lime-oil factory beyond Zapatalito. Shrimp and fish populations are declining. Locals have faced the consequences of diminishing catch and have even demanded government action.

In 2013, local fishermen’s collective, supported by the Human Rights Ombudsman of the People of Oaxaca (DDHPO), produced a report regarding violations against the inhabitants of Zapotalito, Chacahua, La Pastoría and El Corral details the public health risks, loss of livelihood and environmental degradation that communities have faced due to federal infrastructure projects, such as Irrigation District 110 and breakwaters in the Boca de Chacahua.

The resilience of mangroves

Part of a roughly 51-square-mile national park designated in 1937, Chacahua Lagoon is surrounded by a network of mangrove corridors, anchoring the island in verdant, woody tresses. Mangroves are trees or bushes that thrive in brackish tidal waters, often where a river meets the sea, offering nesting grounds for a diversity of wildlife.

The red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle), black mangrove (Avicennia germinans), white mangrove (Laguncularia racemosa), and buttonwood (Conocarpus erectus) are also essential to maintaining the health of the local ecosystem.

Their long, complex root systems are adapted to survive in low-lying waters, optimising oxygen absorption and filtering out saline contamination. They endure conditions that are virtually impossible for other plants, and their resilience is recognized by the locals.

Angél runs a grocery shop in the central square. His family has been living on the island for generations. The salinity of the sea is getting worse, he concedes, but “the mangroves are strong. We don’t have to cut them that much.”

“The mangroves are doing well,” Antonio agrees. “They’re tough. When they fall, they land upright,” due to their roots.

The resilience of locals

Perhaps Antonio and Angél aren’t giving themselves enough credit. In reality, mangroves are vulnerable to climate change, specifically increasing salinity, hurricane events, and worsening El Niño patterns. But it’s the locals who demonstrate climate resilience every day, in working as a community to restore the things that Angél says the government is neglecting financially and administratively.

“The effort is made every day; it’s part of life here on the island,” Augusto says. “People engage in what’s called tequio, voluntary community work to help the environment.”

In the same way, the fishermen are taking it upon themselves to try and mitigate the marine pollution, but there is a limit to what can be done without wider support.

Tequio “takes place because people love their land,” Augusto explains, but as Angél marks, the climate is getting hotter, the sea saltier, and the water warmer.

On top of this, the briny waves of gentrification are lapping at the island’s shores. Lavish cabanas with their polished wood walls and hiked-up rent are beginning to rear their haute heads.

Tourism has also been shown to worsen pollution. In Mexico’s Caribbean coast, the tourism sector accounts for one-third of the region’s total waste, and light pollution has been proven to pose threats to turtle populations, of which species such as the Leatherback are populous in Chacahua.

What’s in store for Chacahua?

Oaxaca has been strongly affected by hurricanes Otis, John, Erick, and Boris in the last four years.

While federal budgeting continues to be an issue for Natural Protected Areas across Mexico, local cooperatives, in tandem with the National Commission of Protected Natural Areas (CONANP), are taking measures to respond to growing tourism in the state of Oaxaca and have made major steps in wildlife protection and sustainable infrastructure, but the direct effects on Chacahua are yet to be comprehensively reported.

Looking into its climate future, Chacahua is standing at a delta. It goes without saying that the community has demonstrated its climate resilience through supporting mangroves, keeping the waters around the island clean, and reconstructing and relocating seafront buildings.

However, without sufficient government support, the effects of environmental jeopardy and injustice may ultimately uproot the mangrove system and local way of life to an irremediable degree.

Millie Deere is a freelance journalist.

World.title: How Múcara became one of Mexico’s best restaurants
World.content:
If you flip through the Guía México Gastronómico — an annual 200-page book that maps a flavorful constellation of Mexico’s most delicious restaurants, from the northernmost corner of Baja California to the southernmost point of Chiapas — you’ll find it: Múcara.

Off the page, the restaurant is located on a steep, narrow road in the historic center of Xalapa, Veracruz, tucked away — somewhat inconspicuously — between a comic shop, a tamalería, apartments, cafés and bars crammed with college students. It’s easy to miss. In fact, if you were to pass by for the first time, you’d likely skip right past it.

And yet, the intimate fonda, which seats a maximum of 20 diners at seven tables, has quietly risen to become among the most notable restaurants in the country — and is the first in Xalapa’s history to garner such prestigious national recognition, as designated by an editorial board of influential food critics, journalists, sommeliers and hospitality experts in Mexico.

How Múcara became a destination eatery

That is, Múcara is one of Mexico’s best places to eat. And they’ve earned it, despite not being in a buzzy or touristic hub of the nation.

Múcara’s objective is clear. Their menu is about retaining and expanding the overlooked culinary lineage of Veracruz through a delicious balance of elevated-yet-homely dishes — highlighting seasonal ingredients, refined cooking techniques and hyper-regional recipes. Strangely, it’s a radical concept in Veracruz’s capital city, where the dominant foods seem to be burgers, wings, pizza and pasta, and where if you were to ask a local where to find the best traditional Xalapeño bites, the list would be brief. That glaring absence is what inspired Múcara to open in 2016, when Lesterloon Sánchez Trinidad, a lifetime Xalapeño and the founding chef behind Múcara, first launched his vision.

“I wanted people to discover the regional foods from this area; Veracruz food is one of the oldest in the world,” says Sánchez Trinidad. “Veracruz includes the Olmec, and this region has been a historical crossing for Europeans, Asians, Arabs and the world. It’s the cradle of Mexican food. But at the national level, Veracruz is very forgotten. Modernity has caused us to spend our time differently and change our techniques in the kitchen. The previous generation is turning off their ovens, and things are rapidly changing. The history is being lost.”

A life-changing dining experience

At Múcara, that history is potent, and edible. And most of it is life-changingly delicious.

For lunch, that might taste like a courtesy apéritif of tepache de limón (a bold, citrusy shot of fermented lime juice) to go along with a glass of agua de acuyo (a refreshingly sweet and herbal dose of pepperleaf extract), anchored by a round of enchiladas encacahuatadas (a rich portion of four enchiladas, made with in-house tortillas that are rolled up and with filled shredded chicken, then bathed in a very mildly spiced peanut mole and blanched peanuts sprinkled atop).

There’s also envueltos de plátano (rolled tortillas, stuffed with mashed bananas and drenched in sweet, chocolatey mole); enmoladas de tlatonile (tortillas with chicken and regional tlatonile sauce, brought over from the nearby mountain town of Huasteco, and accompanied with epazote, a tea plant, and chile compeño, a rare pepper that is cultivated in Comapa, Veracruz).

Salads include a rich fig variety or a native peach criollo option. Another standout is the pasta with huitlacoche (house-made pappardelle pasta mixed with flavorful corn fungi, nata, garlic, onion, aged cheese and a touch of olive oil). The menu is relatively compact in its offerings, but at Múcara, it’s about quality and perfection, rather than empty spectacle. It’s about savoring the basics, rather than seeking the bombastic.

Mixing and matching the menu

Of course, aspects of the menu are constantly in flux, depending on the time of year and what ingredients are available from producers and local markets, making it an interactive dining experience where you can jigsaw yourself into nirvana with just about any combination of plates at your table.

Having studied the culinary arts in Mexico City with some of Mexico’s most prominent chefs as a young cook, Sánchez Trinidad — who is relatively young — has compiled and combined over a decade of experience in the kitchen through trial and error. Initially, he opened Nao as a café and pambassería (a small shop that only sold pambazos, the small sandwich of Xalapeño fame, of which he says were prominent in his upbringing but are no longer seen as commonly around Xalapa). Unfortunately, Nao closed during the pandemic, though its closure allowed him to shift his full attention to Múcara, the more ambitious of his projects. That focus has paid off, as Múcara has converted into a decade-long fixture in the city’s culinary scene.

If you go to Yucatán, you’ll easily find 20 or 30 places to eat Yucatán food,” Sánchez Trinidad tells Mexico News Daily. “Same in Puebla for Poblana food. Or in Oaxaca. But in Xalapa, there’s nothing like that. It’s an interesting case study. How is it possible that as a state capital we don’t even know our own cuisine that well? What are our dishes?”

Old-school Veracruz cuisine made modern

On a drizzly Xalapeño afternoon, you can discover the answer to Sánchez Trinidad’s rhetorical question. Múcara is a refuge for the state’s fading past — a slow-cooking, old-school type of joint in modern digs, where no one is rushing the process for the sake of instant gratification, but instead cherishing each bite and all that it offers and imparts about Veracruz’s diverse history. In many cases, Sánchez Trinidad has pulled recipes from his childhood memories of preparing food with his mother and grandmother. His restaurant isn’t just a love letter to his state; it’s an entire library’s worth.

Elegant yet elemental

As a result of his careful attention and thoughtful choices, the meals are orchestral: simple, yet highly calibrated and masterfully executed, highlighting the contradictory pleasures of Mexican cuisine as being elegantly refined while, simultaneously, retaining its most elemental essences.

“The origin of the name Múcara comes from a rock (fossilized coral and marine sediments) that was taken out of the sea,” Sánchez Trinidad explains. “They made buildings out of that. The oldest buildings in the Veracruz port are made from it. Churches, forts, everything. Those old buildings remain and haven’t fallen, and that’s what we strive to be for Veracruz cuisine.”

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Thank you, Harry Styles: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
A few nights ago, my wife and I watched the movie “Three Amigos” with Steve Martin, Chevy Chase and Martin Short. Even though the movie was first released in 1986 — 40 years ago! — I recently saw a classic clip of them in my social media feed that inspired me to want to watch it again. The clip was of them ordering a beer in a Mexican bar. The bartender says, “We have no beer, only tequila.” They ask, “What is tequila?”, to which the bartender replies, “It’s like beer.” They proceed to do a shot and have a hilarious reaction. Not exactly Emmy award-winning lines and acting, but funny nonetheless.

I understand that the movie is meant to be a parody and not taken too seriously, but I will admit I was surprised at the overt stereotypical imagery used to portray Mexico. Nearly every man shown was dirty, poor and drunk. Nearly every woman shown was poor, sun-burned and disheveled — except, of course, for the few ladies who fell in love with the “three amigos.” The “bad guys” were also drunk and dirty, but also had lots of guns and made a living from robbing people. In addition to the characters, the images of Mexico and Mexican life were about as negatively stereotypical as you could imagine: poor, dusty, lawless, run-down and in the middle of the desert. People hanging around and drinking in the middle of the day, not hesitating to start shooting people. Of course, this is nothing new. Hollywood portrayals of Mexico in this way first began in Western movies in the 1910’s — over 100 years ago!

Again, I know some of you are thinking “lighten up Travis, it’s just a comedy film”. I get that, but the decades of stereotypes about Mexico portrayed in movies have had an impact on people’s perceptions about the country and its people. A few months ago, one of our writers wrote an in-depth article about it here: Stereotypes worth 1,000 words: Mexico’s visualization in the media.

And it’s not just Mexico — other countries suffer the same fate at the whims of Hollywood writers and producers.

In the decades after the “Three Amigos” movie, the Hollywood narrative of Mexico changed from the wild west version to the drug lord/narco version. Countless series were made of the cartel leaders, the cartel lifestyle, with “Narcos” from Netflix being the most popular one. In fact, “Narcos” has been one of the most-viewed series ever produced by Netflix. So, for over one hundred years, Hollywood has presented Mexico (not always, but very frequently) as a dirty, lawless location in a Western movie, and more recently as the home of cartels and the drug trade.

Which brings me to the point of my column today: Thankfully, that image is beginning to change. Not by Hollywood, but by musicians (most of them non-American). Over the past two weeks, I couldn’t help but notice in my social media feed all of the images of U.K. mega-star Harry Styles hanging out and enjoying Mexico City. He is in the city to do six concerts over nearly two weeks, and countless videos of him enjoying the city have been popping up. Jogging in Chapultepec Park, going for walks on the tree-lined streets with his girlfriend, eating tacos, standing in line for breakfast pastries — basically, looking and acting like a local and seemingly enjoying every minute of it.

Harry Styles continúa caminando muy relajado por las calles de la CDMX, a un día de su concierto. 🥹 Confiesen, ¿alguien ya se lo encontró? 👀😍 Video por: alexasaeenz pic.twitter.com/NPJqOXrX7r — EstiloDF (@EstiloDF) July 30, 2026

He is the latest artist to do this, but certainly is not the first. Earlier this year, Colombian-born Shakira did a total of 14 concerts (13 in stadiums + 1 free one in the zocalo) in Mexico City. She was seen for weeks hanging out and enjoying the capital city. Also in the past few months, Irish rock band U2 filmed a music video in the city and took time to visit with President Sheinbaum. And Korean mega-K-pop group BTS did a three-day concert series in the city and were seen hanging out and enjoying the sights, as well as visiting with Sheinbaum. Late last year, Dua Lipa — who is Albanian and grew up in the U.K. — spent a week in Mexico City performing three concerts as well. She was seen dancing in nightclubs, eating late-night tacos, and genuinely enjoying the city she calls “one of her favorites in the world.”

What an incredible change this has been in the portrayal of the country. After decades of Hollywood portrayals of Mexico as a lawless, unsafe, dirty place, you now have real stars genuinely hanging out and having a good time in Mexico. The images appear to be real, genuine, authentic and spontaneous — as different from Hollywood as you can get. It would be easy to have a cynical take on these musicians and simply say that what they are doing is good for their own business. Of course it is, but I would prefer someone making money by getting out, walking around, talking to locals and eating local food rather than presenting a stereotypical, outdated and false narrative.

The World Cup was a similar phenomenon. In the months leading up to the games, the media warned us of the dangers of cartel violence and protests. The reality that we saw was of the visiting fans from Colombia, the U.K., Japan, Korea and many other countries having an absolute blast with locals across the country. It truly felt authentic, which is precisely what made it so fascinating to watch.

So let’s hope that we are beginning to see a new trend of how Mexico is being presented to the rest of the world. If so, I think it will have a hugely positive impact on the country and hopefully finally do away with the negative stereotypes that were so common in past decades.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: KIO Data Centers doubles down on Querétaro with a US $1.3B expansion plan
World.content:
The Mexican data center company KIO will pour more than a billion dollars into Querétaro by 2030 as part of an expansion to meet growing U.S. demand for artificial intelligence and data storage.

KIO will spend up to US $1.3 billion to develop the QR03 project, a new data center in the El Marqués Industrial Park in Querétaro city’s eastern outskirts. The latest expansion is expected to create more than 8,000 jobs, direct and indirect.

The move has reinforced the central state’s position as one of Mexico’s leading digital infrastructure hubs. Almost three quarters of all Mexican data centers are in Querétaro.

KIO Data Centers CEO Octavio Camarena Villalvazo announced the decision during an event led by Querétaro Governor Mauricio Kuri González and Mexico’s Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard Casaubón.

Camarena told the gathering that the new infrastructure is part of the company’s growth strategy in a market where data centers are playing a central role in the digital economy.

“Without world-class data centers, there is no cloud, no smart manufacturing, no digitized data, and no artificial intelligence,” Camarena said.

The company’s growth plan has already made some progress with the recent completion of phases two and three of QRO2—the company’s second facility in the state—with a cumulative spend of US $170 million. It has also run its first data center, QRO1, for nearly two decades.

At the same time, KIO plans to invest over US $200 million in 2026 for projects and expansions across Mexico City, Monterrey, Querétaro, and Guatemala, with the objective of meeting regional demand for cloud and artificial intelligence infrastructure — two segments that have driven up requirements for power capacity and data processing.

Camarena estimated that the company’s project could generate an economic impact of billions of dollars in Mexico due to additional investments. Companies such as AWS, Microsoft, Google Cloud, Equinix, ODATA, CloudHQ, Ascenty, and Huawei have operations, projects, or infrastructure in the state.

A recent projection by the Mexican Association of Data Centers forecast that, by 2031, around US $20 billion would be directly spent on data centers in the country. In addition, it forecast a further US $64 billion in indirect investment, with much of that spent in Querétaro.

With reports from Cluster Industrial, Mexico Industry and El Economista

Foo Fighters have officially booked a Belo Horizonte concert for 18 February 2027. The show lands at Arena MRV as part of their Take Cover Tour 2027.

Foo Fighters Belo Horizonte Show Details and Venue Info

Mark your calendar for Thursday, 18 February 2027. Foo Fighters take the stage at Arena MRV in Belo Horizonte.

Doors open at 4 pm, and the band is scheduled to start at 8 pm local time. The venue sits at Rua Cristina Maria de Assis, 202, in the Bairro Califórnia neighborhood.

This address also serves as the official box office once the general sale begins. Ahead of the general sale, a physical ticket office runs at Arena Hall on Avenida Nossa Senhora do Carmo, 230, in Savassi.

That location handles pre-sale purchases between 17 and 19 August.

Ticket On-Sale Dates and Pre-Sale Schedule for Foo Fighters

The ticketing calendar kicks off with an artist pre-sale on Monday, 17 August. It starts at 10 am online and 11 am at the Arena Hall box office.

This pre-sale is reported by music outlets but is not confirmed in official bank communications. Santander Select and Private Banking clients get their turn on 18 August.

Sales open at 10 am online and 11 am at the box office. The following day, 19 August, opens up to other Santander customers on the same schedule.

General sale goes live at 10 am on 20 August via Ticketmaster Brasil. The official box office at Arena MRV opens at 11 am.

All tickets are 100 percent digital and must be activated through the Quentro app. Each person can buy up to six tickets per CPF, with a maximum of two half-price meia-entrada tickets.

Santander clients can split payments into five interest-free installments. The general public gets up to three.

Doors open at 16:00 on the night. The Arena MRV box office sits at Rua Cristina Maria de Assis, 202, in Califórnia.

Before general sale, the box office runs from a different address. That is Avenida Nossa Senhora do Carmo, 230, in Savassi.

Foo Fighters Ticket Prices in Reais and US Dollar Approximations

Prices span from R$ 280 to R$ 1,180, covering five seating categories at Arena MRV. The cheapest option is Cadeira Superior at R$ 280 for half-price entry, or R$ 560 for a full-price ticket.

Standing-room Pista tickets run R$ 330 half-price and R$ 660 full. The Cadeira Inferior sections, covering Leste, Oeste, and Sul, are listed at R$ 445 half-price and R$ 890 full.

The top tier, Pista Premium Santander Select, costs R$ 590 half-price and R$ 1,180 full. Be aware that some outlets list R$ 445 as a full price for the Inferior sections.

This appears to be an error and is not verified. Converted at the Banco Central PTAX close of R$5.2236 on Friday 14 August 2026, the range is about US$54 to US$226.

These figures are approximations only, as Ticketmaster sells exclusively in Brazilian reais.

Context of the 2027 South American Tour

The Belo Horizonte date sits within a broader South American push for the Take Cover Tour 2027. It was announced separately from the initial stadium leg.

That first announcement on 6 August covered Uruguay, Argentina, Chile, and Peru, with Brazil initially left out. Brazil was added later with two dates: Belo Horizonte on 18 February and São Paulo at MorumBIS on 20 February.

The shows are branded as part of the Take Cover Tour 2027. They did not appear in the original press note.

From Belo Horizonte the run moves to Montevideo on 23 February and Buenos Aires on 25 February. Santiago follows on 28 February and Lima on 3 March 2027.

All shows are stadium dates, with Estadio Centenario, River Plate, Parque Estadio Nacional, and Estadio San Marcos hosting the band. No support act has been announced for the Belo Horizonte or São Paulo dates.

Do not expect an opening lineup just yet. The South American stadium leg does list local acts, but those do not apply to the Brazil shows.

How to Secure Your Tickets for the Foo Fighters Belo Horizonte Show

Your best bet is to buy online through Ticketmaster Brasil, since all tickets are digital and require the Quentro app for entry. Physical box offices handle in-person sales, but the online platform is the only official digital channel.

Santander cardholders get two windows. Select clients buy from 18 August and other clients from 19 August, both at 10 am.

Otherwise, wait for the general sale on 20 August and aim to log in early. Remember that each CPF allows up to six tickets, with only two half-price entries allowed per person.

Payment terms vary, with Santander clients getting up to five interest-free installments and others up to three. Pista Premium Santander Select is the top tier at R$1,180 full price.

A standing spot in Pista costs R$660. If you are on a budget, Cadeira Superior at R$ 560 full price remains a solid option.

Do not rely on unofficial resellers, as tickets are digital and tied to your account. Stick to the official channels and check your Quentro app ahead of the show date.

Brazilian venues sell by CPF, the national taxpayer number. Foreign buyers usually need a CPF or a Brazilian resident to buy on their behalf.

Each CPF can buy up to six tickets, of which no more than two may be half-price. Half-price entry covers students, over-60s and other categories under Brazilian law.

Frequently Asked Questions

When do Foo Fighters play in Belo Horizonte? The concert is on Thursday, 18 February 2027, at Arena MRV. Doors open at 4 pm and the show starts at 8 pm local time. Where can I buy tickets for the Foo Fighters Belo Horizonte show? Tickets are available exclusively through Ticketmaster Brasil online, with physical sales at designated box offices. General sale opens on 20 August at 10 am, with pre-sales running from 17 August. What are the ticket prices for Foo Fighters in Belo Horizonte? Prices range from R$ 280 (about US$ 54) for half-price upper seats to R$ 1,180 (about US$ 226) for premium standing. Full-price tickets go from R$ 560 to R$ 1,180 depending on the category. Is the Belo Horizonte show part of the South American tour? Yes. The Take Cover Tour 2027 also takes in São Paulo, Montevideo, Buenos Aires, Santiago and Lima. The Brazil shows were announced separately from the initial South American stadium leg.

Three food festivals in Rio this month range from a finished barbecue blowout to a free Texas BBQ this weekend. Here’s what’s actually on today and what’s ahead.

If you’re a foreign resident or visitor in Rio this weekend, your barbecue options are slim but not zero. The big churrasco festival, BBQ Sem Fronteiras, wrapped up yesterday with premium cuts and open bar.

Rio food festivals still to come

BBQ Sem Fronteiras took place on Saturday, 15 August 2026, from 13:00 to 21:00. It is not running today.

You can’t attend now, but knowing what happened helps you plan for future editions. The venue was Jockey Club Brasileiro at Praça Santos Dumont, 31, in Gávea.

Tickets ranged from R$90 for kids aged 6–11 to R$560 for adults, bought on Ingresse (ingresse.com). One report mentioned a price of R$520, which likely was an earlier lot.

No official US$ prices were published. An informal conversion at R$5.50/US$ would put R$560 at about US$102, but that’s not confirmed.

The event featured many chefs preparing grilled meats, including cupim with Korean seasoning and a whole lamb from Patagonia. An open bar with draft beer, wine, and cocktails was included, plus desserts by Carola Troisgros.

Expect a premium experience if it returns, as tickets were pricey. For now, your next churrasco chance is the Texas BBQ this weekend, which won’t cost you a cent for entry.

Texas BBQ: Free Churrasco This Weekend in Barra

The Texas BBQ festival runs from Friday, 21 August 2026, through Sunday, 23 August. It takes place at Shopping Metropolitano Barra in the West parking lot, near the Centauro store.

The address is Avenida Embaixador Abelardo Bueno, 1300, in Barra da Tijuca. Admission is completely free, as confirmed by both Veja Rio and Diário do Rio.

That means you can walk in without paying anything, though you might spend on food and drinks inside. Hours differ by day: Friday from 17:00 to 22:00, Saturday from 14:00 to 22:00.

Sunday from 14:00 to 21:00 per Diário do Rio; Veja Rio doesn’t specify the Sunday end time. It’s a fogo de chão style event, featuring slow-roasted meats over embers with various cuts at different stations.

You can also find draft craft beer (chope artesanal), other gastronomy options, and live music all weekend. Given the free entry and family-friendly vibe, this is a solid choice for expats and tourists.

Just get there early on Sunday to catch the full hours.

Mamma Mia!: Italian Food and Grape Stomping, But Dates Unclear

Mamma Mia! is an Italian food festival that brings pizzas, pastas, cheeses, cannoli, gelato, and wines.

It also includes shows and typical dances. Notably, it features a grape stomping (pisa da uva) experience for visitors.

The exact dates for this edition are not fully verified in the sources. O Globo only mentions it as part of a weekend lineup with a Friday–Sunday schedule.

It’s held at the Uptown complex in Barra, but the street address isn’t published in the articles. Opening hours are listed as Friday 17:00–00:00, Saturday 12:00–00:00, and Sunday 12:00–23:00.

However, without specific calendar dates, we cannot confirm if it’s running today. No entry price is published either, so don’t assume it’s free.

The grape stomping is a rare hands-on activity you won’t find at most Rio festivals, so it’s worth tracking down. For now, your safest bet is to treat this as a future option, not a today or this-weekend one.

Keep an eye on O Globo’s RioShow section for updates.

Feira do Podrão: Giant Coxinha and Oversized Snacks

If you’re into over-the-top street food, Feira do Podrão at Carioca Shopping in Vila da Penha is worth remembering. It features a 2 kg coxinha and a 1.20-meter hot dog, among other extravagant snacks.

The festival also has about 30 vendors, plus kids’ activities, DJs, and a samba circle (roda de samba). That makes it a fun outing for families.

However, the exact dates for this edition are not confirmed in the sources—only a generic Friday–Sunday schedule. Hours are listed as Friday 17:00–22:00, Saturday 14:00–22:00, and Sunday 14:00–22:00, but we don’t know if those apply to this specific weekend.

No entry price is published, so we can’t say if it’s free or not. The venue is Carioca Shopping in Vila da Penha, but the full street address isn’t given in the article.

You’ll need to look up the mall’s exact location separately if you decide to go. The giant coxinha is a Brazilian classic, and a 2 kg version is a sight to see.

Don’t plan your day around it until you confirm dates. Check O Globo’s RioShow or the shopping center’s social media for the latest.

Beyond Rio: Grape Harvest Festivals in the Region

If you’re willing to travel, there’s a famous Festa do Vinho e da Uva in Santa Teresa, Espírito Santo. Note it’s not in the city of Rio.

That festival ran from 7 to 9 August 2026, so it’s already finished as of today. It featured a grape stomping event with 500 kg of grapes, making about 250 liters of juice distributed free.

The event was free to enter, organized by the Lions Clube Santa Teresa Colibri, but it’s a 10-hour drive from Rio. There are no other grape harvest festivals in Rio with confirmed dates for August or September 2026 in our sources.

Keep checking local event listings if you want to catch the next pisa da uva experience closer to the city. For now, your realistic options are Texas BBQ for this weekend, and maybe Mamma Mia!

or Feira do Podrão if you can pin down dates. Always confirm hours and prices on official channels before heading out.

The next churrasco event is Texas BBQ, which runs from Friday 21 to Sunday 23 August at Shopping Metropolitano Barra, with free admission. How much does it cost to enter the Texas BBQ? Entry is completely free, as confirmed by multiple sources. You’ll only pay for food and drinks inside, so it’s a budget-friendly way to enjoy Brazilian barbecue. When is the Mamma Mia! Italian festival happening? The exact dates are not published in our sources; only a Friday–Sunday schedule is given. Feira do Podrão at Carioca Shopping in Vila da Penha features a 2 kg coxinha, but the event’s dates are unverified. For any current event, confirm dates and entry fees on official channels.

Medellín: Social Hostels and a Realistic Safety Picture for Solo Travel

A 2026 U.S. travel industry release lists Medellín among Colombia’s top places for solo travel.

It sits alongside Bogotá and Cartagena on that list. Digital-nomad safety coverage from July 2026 says the city is safe enough for thousands to base here.

The local “no dar papaya” rules are not optional. El Poblado and Laureles come up repeatedly as comfortable neighborhoods for foreigners who stay alert.

A July 2026 backpacker guide names several hostels there as “great for solo travelers.” The U.S. State Department advisory for Colombia, last updated March 31, 2026, sits at Level 3.

Reconsider travel due to crime, terrorism, and kidnapping. Some areas, including Arauca and Norte de Santander, carry a Level 4: Do not travel warning.

Medellín itself is not in that highest category. For accommodation, the same July 2026 guide puts dorm beds at COP 30,000 to COP 70,000 per night.

This applies to the main backpacker zones. Casa Almarita in Laureles starts at COP 30,000, while La Familia Hostel Manila in El Poblado starts at COP 35,000.

Florianópolis: Beach Hostels and a Clear Off-Season Window

Floripa, as locals call it, ranks in a top-10 list of safest major Brazilian cities for digital nomads in 2026. This is based on official crime data.

The island’s hostel scene is described as social, with dorms often right on the water. Surfboards are available to borrow, which suits solo travelers.

A July 2026 accommodation guide puts a hostel dorm bed at around €20 per night. That comes to roughly US$22 at an assumed rate of €1 = US$1.10.

Three-star hotels in Centro run €40–70 per night, about US$44–77. All buses pass through there, making transit simple.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office warns against all but essential travel to specific river areas of Amazonas state. The research does not mention any such restriction for Florianópolis or most of Santa Catarina.

That said, the full UK Brazil advisory text was not retrieved. The absence of a warning for Floripa is drawn from a secondary summary.

Treat that as an implication rather than a direct quote from the FCDO. The same July 2026 guide names March, April, and November as the real sweet spot.

Buenos Aires: Central, Walkable, and Cheaper Than You Might Expect

World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Mexico · Travel

Key Facts —Amàre Cancún: Opens 31 October 2026, 429 rooms. Bookings open now. Rates not published. —Kimpton Tres Rios: Opens 22 September 2026, Riviera Maya. Bookings open now. Room count unverified. —Sargassum hauls: Over 105,000 metric tons cleared by 14 August 2026, beating 2025’s record. —Alert status: SEMAR keeps the semáforo red for the region as of 9 August 2026. —Clearest beaches: Isla Contoy, Isla Blanca, Punta Sam, and most north-facing Cancún beaches. —Peak season: August to October is the highest risk; conditions ease gradually from September.

Two new all-inclusive properties open this autumn in the Cancun area. They debut as Quintana Roo clears record sargassum tonnage and the regional alert stays red.

Two new all-inclusive resorts open in the Cancun area this autumn. They are debuting into the worst sargassum season on record.

Sargassum washed ashore on a Caribbean beach. Quintana Roo has cleared more than 105,000 tonnes in 2026, beating last year’s record. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Meet the two new resorts

Amàre Cancún sits in the hotel zone of Cancún. The reports confirm it has 429 suites and rooms.

Its exact street address is not published. You can book through amarehotels.com, hilton.com, the Hilton Honors app, or a preferred travel advisor.

Official nightly rates are not published yet. Third-party listings have circulated figures, but none is an official published rate.

Kimpton Tres Rios Riviera Maya is located near Playa del Carmen in the Riviera Maya. Its room count and full address are not confirmed in any public source yet.

Reservations for Kimpton Tres Rios opened in July 2026 through the brand’s booking system. Nightly rates are not published.

A secondary listing quoted a lower figure, but the hotel has not published a rate. Both are all-inclusive brands, but neither property publishes a sargassum-free claim.

We found no source showing either hotel marketing itself that way.

The honest sargassum picture

By 14 August 2026, officials in Quintana Roo had cleared more than 105,000 metric tons of sargassum this year. That already exceeds the previous full-year record of about 92,783 tons set in 2025.

An earlier report from 30 July cited 96,151 tons collected. The over-105,000 figure comes from Reuters on 14 August.

The Mexican Navy, SEMAR, keeps the regional semáforo, or traffic-light alert, in red because of excessive seaweed. The alert was still red as of 9 August 2026.

The season typically peaks in August, September, and October. Coordinator Esteban Amaro of the monitoring network expects significant arrivals to continue into October.

A gradual decline usually begins in late August or September, but it does not happen evenly across all beaches. Some stretches stay heavy while others clear up.

The 2026 season is already the most intense ever measured in the region by tonnage removed. The same August reporting says SEMAR kept the semáforo red for the entire region due to excessive sargassum.

Which beaches are least and worst affected

The clearest water in mid-August tends to be on the north-facing bay side of Cancún. Beaches like Playa Caracol, Playa Langosta, Playa Tortugas, and Playa Las Perlas are consistently among the least affected.

A 2026 summary on Cancun beach conditions states these are on the north side, not the exposed east coast. Isla Contoy, Isla Blanca, and Punta Sam were also clear in monitoring reports from 11 August.

Isla Mujeres beaches including Playa Norte also tested green or blue on that day. The worst stretches by early August included Tulum Zona Hotelera, Akumal, Puerto Aventuras, Playa del Carmen, and Mahahual.

Puerto Morelos Norte was specifically listed as red on 10–12 August reporting. Punta Allen, Punta Pájaros, and Xcalak had excessive sargassum in the 7 August network report.

Those beaches face the open Caribbean and get little natural protection. Check the Red de Monitoreo map one or two days before you travel, because conditions shift quickly.

A beach that is clear today can be brown tomorrow. The monitoring network showed 56 of 140 beaches in red on 7 August.

When it eases and what you should do

The safest booking window for clearer beaches is late January through April. November to early December is also lower-risk, but no month is guaranteed clean.

Esteban Amaro said the season would likely continue for a couple more months with a larger decline toward September or October. If you book for late 2026, choose a north-facing beach in Cancún, Costa Mujeres, or Isla Mujeres.

Those locations have the best odds through the tail of the season. Avoid Tulum, Akumal, and Playa del Carmen for an autumn trip if seaweed is your main concern.

Those beaches are the most exposed and the slowest to clear. Ask your hotel directly about its cleanup schedule and whether it runs boats with barriers.

Hotel-level effort matters and is not always counted in official totals. Consider travel insurance that covers cancellation for natural conditions.

No resort can promise sargassum-free water, so protect your booking.

What authorities are doing about it

The federal government announced a MX$2.635 billion strategy for Quintana Roo. That is about US$155 million at 17.02 pesos to the dollar on 16 August 2026.

That plan includes two tugboats, six coastal collection vessels, and nearly 51 kilometers of barriers. The first phase of that plan is worth MX$768.7 million, about US$45 million.

Collection capacity is meant to rise from 1,227 tons per day to 1,870 tons per day. The Navy also operates 11 coastal ships, one amphibious collector, 18 support boats, and four drones across the region.

The state government allocated another MX$770 million, about US$45 million, to strengthen satellite monitoring. Playa del Carmen separately plans a 5-kilometer offshore barrier funded with MX$45 million (about US$2.6 million).

Municipal crews clean public beaches while hotels run their own teams. Hotel cleanups often do not appear in the official tonnage figures.

The federal strategy aims to raise capacity to 4,000 tons per day by 2027. None of this prevents the seaweed from arriving; it only removes it faster once it does.

That is why the alert can stay red even on busy tourism days.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it safe to book a Cancun resort for autumn 2026? Yes, but choose your beach carefully. North-facing Cancún beaches and Isla Mujeres have the best odds of clearer water through October. Avoid Tulum and Playa del Carmen if sargassum is a dealbreaker for you. Check the Red de Monitoreo map before booking. Do the new resorts promise sargassum-free beaches? No. Neither Amàre Cancún nor Kimpton Tres Rios publishes such a claim, and we found no source showing they do. Treat any such promise with suspicion. When does the sargassum season normally end? Arrivals usually decline from late August or September, but heavy events can continue into October and November. The safest window for travel is January through April. How bad is 2026 compared with previous years? It is the worst on record so far. More than 105,000 metric tons had been removed by 14 August, already surpassing the 2025 full-year record of about 92,783 tons.

Key Facts —Best all-around: Jardins or Pinheiros. —Business hubs: Itaim Bibi or Vila Olímpia. —Quiet living: Higienópolis. —Budget choice: Centro, with street-awareness. —Nightlife: Vila Madalena. —Metro: Line 6 partially open as of July 2026.

A foreign visitor or new expat faces a tough choice among São Paulo’s neighborhoods. Here’s an honest comparison of the main areas, who they suit, and the trade-offs.

Arriving in São Paulo, you face a big question: where to live. The city’s neighborhoods each offer a distinct rhythm and set of trade-offs.

Street art in Vila Madalena, one of the São Paulo neighborhoods most popular with visitors. The district sits on Metro Line 2-Green. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

São Paulo Neighborhoods: Jardins, Polished and Central

Jardins is upscale, central, and packed with restaurants and retail. It is a loose guidebook term, not a formal census unit, covering parts of Jardim Paulista and Cerqueira César.

The area suits first-time visitors, business travelers, and expats who want a polished base near Paulista Avenue. Crime stats are not reported under the Jardins label, so safety data is unverified for the area.

The nearest metro is Line 2-Verde, with Trianon-Masp or Consolação stations, though exact distances are unverified. Hotel WZ Jardins sits at Av. Rebouças, 955, Jardim Paulista, São Paulo, SP 05401-100.

The ibis budget São Paulo Jardins is at Avenida Nove De Julho 3597. Average rates run around R$239, with deals from R$184, per KAYAK and momondo listings.

The exact rate in US dollars is not published in the sources. This neighborhood offers a seamless introduction to the city.

It balances urban energy with a more relaxed atmosphere. The area feels walkable and convenient for cultural spots and high-end dining.

The reputation is well-earned, but it comes at a price, so budget-conscious travelers should compare options carefully.

São Paulo Neighborhoods: Pinheiros, Local and Lively

Pinheiros is dense and mixed-use, with major office and dining corridors. It suits expats who want restaurants, transport access, and a more local daily-life feel.

The neighborhood saw 1,473 robberies from January to May 2026, up 8% year over year, per a 2026 operator guide. That sounds alarming, but it is lower than some other districts when adjusted for size.

The nearest metro is Line 4-Amarela, with Faria Lima or Pinheiros stations. Exact walking times are unverified.

Hotel rates in Pinheiros are not published in our sources. The area is known for its food-and-culture corridor, attracting young professionals.

It has a more authentic feel compared to tourist-heavy zones. Despite the robbery numbers, many locals consider it vibrant and safe during the day.

Nighttime caution is advised, as with any big city. The district’s infrastructure is improving, with better sidewalks and lighting.

This helps make it more pedestrian-friendly over time. There are plenty of parks and cultural venues nearby, adding to the overall quality of life for residents.

São Paulo Neighborhoods: Itaim Bibi and Vila Olímpia for Business

Itaim Bibi is an affluent business district with offices, hotels, and restaurants. Corporate travelers and higher-budget expats prioritize convenience over atmosphere here.

A 2026 safety guide ranks it below some higher-robbery districts, but gives no specific figure for Itaim Bibi. Access to Lines 5-Lilás and 9-Esmeralda is common, with Cidade Jardim or Faria Lima as likely stations, depending on your street.

Hotel prices here are not published in our research. Vila Olímpia is a modern office-and-apartment district with malls, gyms, and nightlife.

It suits short-stay business visitors and expats who want modern towers and corporate convenience. The nearest metro is Line 9-Esmeralda’s Vila Olímpia station, though exact details are unverified.

Both areas are close to major corporate hubs, like Faria Lima Avenue. This makes them ideal for executives with meetings in the financial district.

Safety in Vila Olímpia is unverified, but the modern infrastructure suggests a managed environment. It is generally considered safe for day-to-day activities.

Housing options include luxury apartments and serviced suites, catering to short stays. The nightlife is upscale, with chic bars and clubs in both districts.

São Paulo Neighborhoods: Vila Madalena and Higienópolis

Vila Madalena is bohemian and nightlife-focused, with a strong residential feel. It suits younger expats and remote workers who want walkability and a strong bar scene.

The closest metro is Line 2-Verde, with Vila Madalena station, though exact details are unverified. Higienópolis, by contrast, is older and quieter.

It has a traditional, residential feel that suits families and longer-stay expats. It is near Line 4-Amarela, with the Higienópolis-Mackenzie station.

A future Line 6-Laranja station, Higienópolis Mackenzie, is planned but not yet open, per 2026 metro news. Hotel rates in both areas are not published in our sources.

Vila Madalena’s streets are lined with vibrant street art and independent shops. It is a haven for creatives, with a strong community vibe.

It can be noisy on weekends, which might not suit everyone. Higienópolis offers a more tranquil pace, with tree-lined streets and historic buildings.

It is close to universities, adding a scholarly atmosphere, and appeals to those who appreciate classic architecture. Families often choose it for safety and good schools.

São Paulo Neighborhoods: the Trade-off of Centro

Centro is the historic core with architecture, transit, and institutions. The day-to-day environment is the most uneven for newcomers.

It suits budget travelers and those who need very central access, but requires strong street-awareness. The Sé district, part of Centro, saw 1,027 robberies from January to May 2026, per the 2026 guide.

Metro access is excellent, with Sé, São Bento, and República stations nearby, though exact routes are unverified. Hotel rates here are not published in our research.

The area boasts landmarks like the Municipal Theatre and São Bento Monastery. During the day, it is bustling with office workers and shoppers.

At night, it can feel empty and less safe, so extra caution is required. Budget options are scarce in our sources, but the area has many low-cost hostels.

Public transport links are unmatched, making it easy to explore the whole city. The architecture is stunning, with colonial and modernist styles mixed.

However, homelessness and petty crime are visible, which can be jarring. If you are resilient and street-smart, Centro can be affordable, but expect a more challenging environment.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the safest neighborhood in São Paulo for a foreigner? No neighborhood is uniformly safe. The 2026 guide warns that labels like Jardins are not formal reporting units. Pinheiros and Sé have higher robbery counts, but safer areas like Itaim Bibi lack specific data. Which area has the best metro access for a newcomer? Centro offers multiple lines (1, 3, and future 6), while Jardins and Pinheiros sit on Line 2-Verde. Itaim Bibi and Vila Olímpia connect via Lines 5-Lilás and 9-Esmeralda. Are there budget hotel options in these neighborhoods? Yes, the ibis budget São Paulo Jardins offers rates from R$184, with an average of R$239. The dollar rate is not published in our sources, and other areas’ prices are not published either. What’s new with São Paulo’s metro in 2026? Line 6-Laranja opened its first phase on July 2, 2026. It runs free during weekdays from 10:00 to 15:00. Full paid service is planned by end-2026, with future stations including Higienópolis.

Why Cartagena de Indias Made the Best in Travel 2026 List

Lonely Planet’s Best in Travel 2026, published in October 2025 per secondary reports, highlights 25 destinations for the year ahead. Cartagena’s inclusion at number 20 comes from its well-preserved Spanish colonial architecture, as reported by Semana.

Summaries also highlight its vibrant food and nightlife culture. The walled old town, built during the 16th century, sits in the city center.

Cobblestone lanes and colorful balconies line its streets. The fortifications stretch for 11 kilometers along the coast.

They offer views of the Caribbean Sea. Beyond history, Cartagena’s restaurant scene in Getsemaní and Bocagrande serves fresh ceviche and modern Caribbean fusion.

The city also hosts festivals like the International Music Festival in January, though this event is not part of the cited coverage. Colombian outlet Semana confirmed the 20th ranking among the 25 best destinations in the world.

Note that Lonely Planet’s own page has not been directly verified for this article. The rank relies on third-party reporting.

How to Get to Cartagena de Indias

You will fly into Rafael Núñez International Airport, the city’s main gateway for international and domestic flights. Direct flights from Bogotá’s El Dorado Airport take about 1 hour and 30 minutes.

This makes it an easy hop from the capital city. This flight duration is standard airline timetable data, not from the Best in Travel 2026 coverage.

The airport lies roughly 5 kilometers from the old town walls, based on general geography. A taxi ride from the airport is common, but costs are not published in the current sources.

Many visitors also arrive by bus from Santa Marta or by cruise ship. Cartagena is a major Caribbean port, though bus specifics are not detailed in cited articles.

Remember to exchange money at the airport or use ATMs in the city. Credit card acceptance is not universal in smaller shops, which is practical travel advice, not from cited articles in the research set.

What to Do in Cartagena de Indias

Start with the Old Town, where you can walk the 16th-century ramparts at the Baluarte de Santo Domingo. Explore plazas like Plaza de la Aduana, which are central to the city’s historic charm.

Don’t miss the Castillo San Felipe de Barajas, the massive fortress on Cerro de San Lázaro. It offers panoramic views of the city and harbor, as commonly known in travel literature.

Exact street addresses for these sites are not present in the retrieved sources. Confirm them locally before visiting, as the research set does not publish them.

Barrio Getsemaní, just south of the old town, is the place for street art. Local food stalls cluster at Plaza de la Trinidad, with a lively nightlife scene nearby.

For a beach day, take a short boat ride to the Rosario Islands, located about 40 kilometers offshore. Boats depart from the pier at Muelle de la Bodeguita, a typical departure point.

The Gold Museum (Museo del Oro Zenú) showcases pre-Columbian gold artifacts. This is a widely known attraction, but its address is not from the cited sources.

Another option is a chiva bus tour. This open-sided vehicle travels through the city streets with live music and dancing.

It offers a fun way to see the highlights at night, per common travel advice. For a fuller experience, consider a walking tour of the old town’s fortifications.

You can learn about the city’s pirate history and the naval battles that shaped its walls. The San Felipe fortress, completed in 1657, was built to repel attacks.

Its tunnels were a military asset, and they now intrigue visitors exploring the site. A sunset stroll along the 11-kilometer coastline is a must.

You will see the city glow as evening sets in, and you can watch ships enter the harbor.

What It Costs to Visit Cartagena de Indias

This coverage does not publish current hotel rates, restaurant prices, taxi fares, tour prices, or attraction fees for Cartagena. The available sources focus on Lonely Planet’s list recognition, not local cost breakdowns.

Readers should check booking sites and local providers directly for up-to-date pricing in Colombian pesos or US dollars. Costs vary widely by season and provider.

For example, budget and luxury options exist across the city, but specific figures are unverified here. Always confirm prices before booking to avoid surprises.

It is wise to carry small bills, as many small shops do not accept credit cards. This is practical advice, not sourced from the cited articles.

When to Visit Cartagena de Indias

The best months to visit are December through March, when the weather is dry. The Caribbean heat is more manageable during these winter months.

This is also the high season, so expect larger crowds. Flights and hotel prices also rise during this period.

This is general climate guidance. It is not explicitly from the Best in Travel 2026 coverage.

April to June and September to November offer fewer tourists and lower rates. You may see brief afternoon showers during these wetter months.

The city’s festivals, like the Hay Festival in January, add extra appeal. The International Music Festival also takes place in January.

These events are not detailed in the cited sources. If you plan to visit during high season, book your accommodation at least 3 months in advance.

This secures availability. Low season may offer discounts on room rates, but check weather forecasts for rain.

The Caribbean climate means warm temperatures year-round. Even in wet months, the sun often breaks through, so you can still explore the city and beaches.

Late afternoon showers are common, so plan outdoor activities for morning hours. This practical tip helps you make the most of your trip, though it isn’t from the cited articles.

If you’re looking to avoid crowds, consider a visit in November. The weather is still good, and the rains have mostly passed, leaving beaches inviting and streets less crowded.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Cartagena safe for tourists? Cartagena is generally safe for tourists, but you should take standard precautions. Avoid empty streets at night and use registered taxis. The U.S. State Department advises increased caution in Colombia due to crime. Check their latest advisory before traveling, as this is not from the current sources. Do I need a visa to visit Cartagena? Most U.S., Canadian, and EU citizens do not need a visa for tourism stays under 90 days. You will need a valid passport with at least six months of validity. This is standard travel information, not from the cited articles. Is Cartagena expensive compared to other Colombian cities? Cartagena is more touristy than Bogotá or Medellín, so prices are higher. Accommodation and tours cost more here. Still, it’s a bargain by North American or European standards, based on general market comparisons. What is the best way to get around Cartagena? The old town is walkable, but for longer trips, taxis are affordable. Ride-sharing apps like Uber also operate in the city. You can also rent a bike or take the local ‘chiva’ bus, per common travel advice. This is not detailed in the retrieved sources.

Why Arteaga Gets the ‘Mexican Switzerland’ Tag

Snow can cap peaks like La Viga and La Martha. Those peaks sometimes hold snow into the early spring.

The comparison is about landscape, not culture. You get mountain scenery reminiscent of the Alps.

The Bosques de Monterreal resort even claims the title of the country’s only ski center, with runs and artificial snow. The town itself remains genuinely Mexican with a parish church, apple orchards, and a mummy museum.

It is a nickname that mostly checks out for nature lovers, though you will not find any fondue here. The apple orchards supply 80% of the state’s fruit, so the agricultural life is real.

The nickname has to do mainly with its mountain and forest surroundings, which recall alpine landscapes. That is why the SECTUR description mentions ‘el viento fresco’ at any hour of the day.

Coahuila’s tourism officials list Arteaga among eight Pueblos Mágicos in the state, along with Parras de la Fuente and Cuatro Ciénegas. The designation is confirmed, but the exact declaration year is not published in public sources.

For a true alpine feel, head to the Sierra de Arteaga. There, pine and oak forests break the surrounding semi-desert, creating a cool microclimate that surprises first-time visitors.

Getting There and the Best Time to Go

From Saltillo, the drive to the sierra area is a short hop of about 15–16 kilometers. That trip takes 15–20 minutes under normal traffic, so you can easily do a day trip from the state capital.

You will take Federal Highway 57, then switch to State Highway 106 heading toward Arteaga. Exact drive times from Monterrey are not published in official sources, so add extra time if you come from the north.

Plan for a longer journey south on the highway. For the full ‘Switzerland’ effect, target autumn or winter, roughly October through February.

December and January offer the best odds of seeing actual snow on the peaks. The tourism profile for Bosques de Arteaga specifically notes ‘nieve dic-ene’ as the snow window.

If you drive from Mexico City, the route covers about 817–820 kilometers via Querétaro, San Luis Potosí, Matehuala, and then Coahuila. That is a solid 9–10 hour drive with tolls.

Always check road conditions in winter. Snow and ice can close mountain segments, so carry chains and drive slowly.

What to Do Beyond the Views

The main draw is Bosques de Monterreal, a mountain resort at 2,900 meters above sea level. Some sources call it the country’s only ski center, with runs that use artificial snow when natural snow is absent.

Even without skiing, the area is perfect for hiking, mountain biking, and just breathing in the forest air. In town, visit the Iglesia de San Isidro Labrador, a parish church that anchors the main square.

Do not miss the Museo de las Momias de Arteaga, which houses naturally mummified remains. It is a quirky stop that adds a cultural layer to your mountain trip.

The municipality also boasts wineries like Vinícolas Los Cedros and Bodegas del Viento. You can add a wine tasting to your mountain itinerary, pairing local vintages with the cool climate.

For birdwatchers, the Santuario del Taray protects a nesting site for the endangered eastern serrana parrot. This is a rare opportunity to see that species in the wild.

The La Acequia, an old water channel, offers a short historical walk near the town center. It is a low-effort way to stretch your legs after the drive.

Where to Stay and What It Costs

Arteaga’s accommodation scene revolves around cabins, with around 60 registered options from simple wood lodges to glamping setups. You will find everything from basic cabins to more resort-style complexes like Bosques de Arteaga.

Operators in the Arteaga sierra do not publish nightly rates online, so we do not publish a rate here. Readers should contact operators directly for current pricing and availability.

Expect higher rates in December, especially during holiday weeks. Book ahead for winter weekends and confirm any minimum-stay requirements.

Many cabins require a minimum stay of two nights during peak periods, so plan your itinerary accordingly. Always confirm cancellation policies to avoid surprises.

If you prefer a hotel, the town of Arteaga itself has a few small options, but most visitors choose the sierra cabins. For a budget stay, consider Saltillo and commute daily, as the drive is only 20 minutes.

Remember that many cabins are self-catering. There are no full-service restaurants on site, so carry groceries from Saltillo or stock up at local shops in Arteaga.

The Practical Details You Need

Plan for cool weather even in summer. The Monterreal area sits at about 2,900 meters, where fresh winds dominate at any hour.

Even in July, daytime highs rarely exceed 20°C, and nights are brisk. Pack layers and a warm jacket for the evenings, especially outside summer months.

Remember that while tourist infrastructure exists, this is a working mountain community, so do not expect 24-hour services. A car is essential for exploring the sierra.

Fill your tank in Saltillo before heading up the mountain roads, as fuel stations are scarce in the high country. Cell phone reception can be patchy in the canyons.

Download offline maps and tell someone your planned route, especially if you hike on remote trails. The altitude might affect visitors from lowland areas.

Take it easy on your first day, drink plenty of water, and avoid heavy meals until you acclimatize. Respect the environment by sticking to marked trails and packing out all trash.

The pine forests are fragile, and local authorities enforce fines for littering.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Arteaga really like Switzerland? You get the pine forests, mountains, and winter snow that inspire the nickname. It is a Mexican mountain town, not an Alpine replica. Set expectations for rustic charm, not cable cars. How far is Arteaga from Saltillo? The drive is about 15–16 kilometers and takes roughly 15–20 minutes from Saltillo. Follow Federal Highway 57 and then State Highway 106. When is the best time to see snow in Arteaga? Aim for winter, specifically December and January. Sources cite this period for natural snow on the peaks. Can you ski in Arteaga? Some sources describe Bosques de Monterreal as the country’s only ski center with runs and artificial snow. Conditions vary, and it is not a large resort.

World.title: Tomás Jofré: The Asado Town That Only Opens at Weekends and on Holidays
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Argentina · Travel

Key Facts —Where: Tomás Jofré, partido of Mercedes, Buenos Aires province. Official GPS name: Jorge Born. —Distance: About 100 km from Buenos Aires city, roughly 1 hour 15 minutes via Acceso Oeste and RN5. —Opening days: 15 of 19 restaurants open only Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays. One serves midweek. —Hours: Kitchens close 17:00–19:00; only Silvano, Fronteras, and La Casona serve dinner (Fri/Sat). —Price: ARS 35,000–45,000 per adult (about US$23–30 at the 14 Aug 2026 Banco Nación rate of 1,515/US$). —Format: Tenedor libre — one fixed price covers picada, pasta, asado, and dessert, usually with drinks.

A 100-km drive from Buenos Aires, this tiny town’s 19 restaurants open almost exclusively on weekends and holidays. Monday 17 August is your rare weekday chance — but arrive early and check the hours.

Monday 17 August is a national holiday in Argentina, Paso a la Inmortalidad del General San Martín. That makes Tomás Jofré worth a special trip.

Gauchos rest with their horses on the Buenos Aires pampas, the countryside that surrounds Tomás Jofré. The town has 264 residents and about 20 restaurants. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)
