What and where is Tomás Jofré

The holiday turns a normal Monday into a golden opportunity for an asado day trip. You’ll join thousands of others doing the same thing, so plan ahead.

A local operator told the press that about 7,000 visitors show up on a typical Sunday. Expect similar numbers this Monday, so arrive by 12:30 to get a table.

The good news is that most restaurants — 15 of the 19 — open their doors on holidays just like weekends. The catch is that if you try on a regular Monday, everything is shut.

Monday 17 August commemorates General José de San Martín, Argentina’s liberator. Banks, schools, and many offices close for the day.

This creates a rare midweek window for people who cannot visit on weekends. Families flock to the countryside for a long lunch.

The town’s rhythm is built around these dates. Restaurants prepare extra meat and fresh pasta for the expected crowds.

Getting There by Car or Train

Drive from Buenos Aires city on Acceso Oeste, then Ruta Nacional 5, and turn at KM 91.5 onto Ruta Provincial 41. The town is about 100 km away, and the trip takes roughly 1 hour 15 minutes.

No passenger train serves Tomás Jofré directly. The tourist train from Mercedes has been suspended since May 2024, when a truck wrecked the bridge over RP41.

Your public transport option is the Línea Sarmiento from Once station, changing at Moreno for the Moreno–Mercedes branch. From Mercedes, 12 km away, grab a taxi or remis to the town.

Take the Acceso Oeste from the city toward Luján. Continue to RN5 and follow signs for Mercedes.

At kilometre 91.5, turn onto RP41. You will see the town entrance a few minutes later.

The road is well-paved and suitable for any car. GPS users should search for ‘Jorge Born’ for the official location.

Allow extra time on holiday mornings because traffic increases. Many visitors leave the city between 9:00 and 11:00.

What to Eat and What It Costs

The format is tenedor libre or a fixed cubierto. One price covers a picada, homemade pasta, asado al asador, and dessert, typically with drinks included.

You won’t find à la carte here. La Querencia de Jofré publishes ARS 45,000 per adult on its own website.

Children aged 6 to 10 pay half, and under-sixes eat free. La Catalina de Jofré’s ‘menú día de campo’ was reported at ARS 35,000 per person in March 2026.

Convert at the Banco Nación selling rate of 1,515 pesos to the dollar, quoted on Friday 14 August 2026. That is about US$23 to US$30 a head.

This is remarkable value for a multi-course meal with drinks. The picada typically includes local cheeses, cold cuts, and salame quintero.

Homemade pasta features sorrentinos, ravioli, or tallarines. The asado al asador is the centrepiece, cooked slowly over wood.

You get a generous portion of beef or pork, often with chorizo and morcilla. Dessert is usually a homemade flan, chocotorta, or fresh fruit.

Coffee and a digestive complete the experience. Salame quintero is a cured salami made by quinteros — Italian market-gardener smallholders of the Mercedes district.

It’s a local pride, celebrated every September in Mercedes.

Restaurant Hours and Names

Silvano opens Friday and Saturday 12:00–16:00 and 20:30–23:00, and Sunday/holidays 12:00–18:00. Fronteras runs Friday 12:00–16:00 and 19:00–00:00, Saturday 8:00–00:00, and Sunday/holidays 9:00–19:00.

Santa Victoria, Antenor, and La Florinda open Saturday, Sunday, and holidays with midday hours: Santa Victoria 11:00–17:00, Antenor 10:00–17:00, La Florinda 11:30–18:00. Reina Mora opens only on Sundays.

La Querencia de Jofré is your only midweek bet, serving Tuesday to Sunday at midday and evening. Santa Victoria takes weekday bookings for pasta only, and Cua Cuá opens other days by reservation.

For dinner on a Friday or Saturday, only Silvano, Fronteras, and La Casona stay open into the evening. On a holiday Monday, don’t count on dinner — most kitchens close by 19:00.

Other names include La Tata, El Rincón de Jofré, and Don Mario. All follow the same holiday pattern.

Most places close completely between 17:00 and 19:00. Arrive before 13:00 for the best selection of tables.

Festivals and Nearby Mercedes

The 9th Fiesta de la Galleta de Campo happened on Sunday 9 August 2026, so you just missed it. But the 51st Fiesta Nacional del Salame Quintero runs 11–13 September 2026 in Mercedes, a 12-km drive away.

Mercedes, the partido capital, offers more dining and a historic center if you want to extend your trip. Just remember that on a holiday Monday, most of Tomás Jofré’s restaurants are open.

They close early, and everything else in town is shut. Plan for a long lunch, not an evening out.

Arrive by 12:30 and eat until 17:00. Then enjoy the quiet countryside before driving back in the late afternoon.

The September festival in Mercedes features salame tastings, cooking demos, and folk music. It draws thousands of visitors from across the province.

If you plan a longer weekend, book a cabin or estancia stay near Mercedes. This lets you enjoy both the festival and the asado town.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Tomás Jofré open on regular weekdays? No, 15 of its 19 restaurants open only on Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays. La Querencia de Jofré is the only place serving midweek, Tuesday to Sunday, so a non-holiday Monday means everything is closed. How much does a meal cost in Tomás Jofré? Expect to pay ARS 35,000 to 45,000 per adult at the fixed-price restaurants. That is about US$23 to US$30 at the 14 August 2026 rate of 1,515 pesos to the dollar. Can I get there by train from Buenos Aires? No direct train goes to the town; the tourist train from Mercedes has been suspended since May 2024. Take the Línea Sarmiento to Mercedes, then a taxi or remis for the last 12 km. What is the food like in Tomás Jofré? The typical format is tenedor libre: one price covers a picada, homemade pasta, asado al asador, and dessert, usually with drinks. Specialties include galleta de campo and salame quintero.

World.title: Novak Djokovic Reveals Health Issue After Cincinnati Open Loss
World.content:
Novak Djokovic’s return to competition lasted just one match Saturday as the 24-time Grand Slam champion struggled physically in the Cincinnati heat before suffering a stunning second-round loss to Argentina’s Thiago Agustin Tirante. The bigger concern came afterward. Djokovic said an ongoing health condition that has troubled him for several years was aggravated by the hot and humid conditions at the Cincinnati Open, raising questions about his physical condition with the US Open approaching.

The 39-year-old Serbian appeared in control early, taking the opening set 6-2 against Tirante. But the match changed dramatically in the second set as Djokovic began showing visible signs of physical distress. At several points, Djokovic bent over between points and struggled to recover after long rallies. He received medical attention after an exhausting service game early in the second set, when tournament medical staff assessed him during the changeover.

“It’s just a condition that I have, health wise, that has been bothering me for the past couple of years,” Djokovic said after the match. He explained that hot and humid weather can make the problem worse. Tirante took advantage as Djokovic’s level dropped, winning the second set 6-4 before staying with the Serbian through a tight deciding set.

Djokovic repeatedly fought his way out of trouble. He saved 13 of the 15 break points he faced during the two-hour, 44-minute match, but Tirante finally broke through with the deciding set tied at 4-4. The Argentine then served out the biggest victory of his career at love, completing a 2-6, 6-4, 6-4 upset.

For Tirante, the victory continued a breakout season. The 25-year-old entered Cincinnati at a career-high No. 50 in the ATP rankings and has now compiled a remarkable 4-1 record against Top 10 opponents. His 2026 season has also included victories over Ben Shelton in Munich and Taylor Fritz in Montreal.

Djokovic, meanwhile, was playing his first match since losing to Jannik Sinner in the Wimbledon semifinals. Cincinnati was expected to give him valuable hard-court competition before the US Open. Instead, his early departure leaves the Serbian with another extended break before the season’s final Grand Slam.

Djokovic remains one of the biggest threats at the majors despite reducing his tournament schedule as he has gotten older. But Saturday’s match provided another reminder that physical recovery has become an increasingly important part of the equation. The conditions in Cincinnati were particularly demanding.

Djokovic’s struggles became obvious during an 18-minute service game early in the second set. He managed to save four break points and hold serve but required medical attention immediately afterward. He continued competing and appeared to recover somewhat during the third set, but Tirante stayed patient.

At 4-4, Djokovic saved three more break points before Tirante finally converted his fourth opportunity. The Argentine then closed out the match without dropping another point. The defeat ended Djokovic’s 10-match Cincinnati Open winning streak. He won the tournament in 2018, 2020 and 2023 and owns a 45-13 career record at the event. Saturday also marked his 139th Masters 1000 appearance, tying Feliciano Lopez for the most in series history.

It may also have been Djokovic’s final appearance in Cincinnati. Asked whether he expected to return to the tournament next year, Djokovic left the possibility open but sounded doubtful. “I certainly hope so, but it looks more likely not, unfortunately,” he said.

For now, attention shifts toward his recovery and preparation for New York. Djokovic has built much of the later stage of his career around arriving at Grand Slam tournaments physically ready to compete for titles. Cincinnati was supposed to be an important part of that preparation.

Instead, he leaves Ohio after one physically punishing match and with more questions surrounding his condition than when he arrived. Tirante advances to face Spain’s Martin Landaluce in the third round.

World.title: Costa Rica Beach Overwhelmed by Trash Flowing Down Tárcoles River
World.content:
A Pacific beach with the potential to attract tourists has instead become one of the clearest examples of Costa Rica’s struggle with waste, as garbage carried down the Tárcoles River continues to wash ashore at Guacalillo Beach. About 90 minutes from San José, Guacalillo sits near the mouth of the Tárcoles, where waste carried from the Greater Metropolitan Area (GMA) reaches the Pacific Ocean.

Plastic bottles, pieces of cardboard, glass and other household garbage collect along the sand and surrounding vegetation. Volunteers have also encountered syringes, shoe soles, cosmetics, utensils and other discarded objects. Much of the problem begins far from the coast. Garbage discarded improperly in the Central Valley can enter streams and rivers that eventually feed into the Tárcoles.

The river then carries the waste west toward Puntarenas, where currents and tides deposit part of it along Guacalillo and nearby beaches. The result is a frustrating cycle for both those who live there and environmental groups. Volunteers remove bags of garbage, only for new debris to arrive with the river, particularly during periods of heavy rainfall.

Community members and organizations now have cleanup efforts at least every weekend, spending hours collecting and separating waste from the sand, driftwood and vegetation. The contamination presents an especially difficult challenge for a community that would like Guacalillo to become better known as a tourism destination. Instead of beachgoers, stretches of shoreline can be dominated by accumulated trash and scavenging birds.

There are now efforts to build a more permanent response. At the end of July, Guacalillo opened Puntarenas province’s first Beach Cleanup and Volunteer Center, designed to support waste collection, environmental education and organized volunteer work. The facility was developed in response to the persistent amount of garbage reaching the area through the Tárcoles.

The center includes areas for training and volunteer activities, as well as a native-plant nursery for reforestation, a plastic museum intended to promote environmental education and a protected area for sea turtle eggs from turtles nesting along the beach. Organizers also hope to recover materials that can still be reused while finding alternatives for harder-to-process waste. Some plastics can be recovered, while materials such as tires and textiles may potentially be transformed for use in asphalt or construction materials.

The scale of the broader waste problem, however, remains significant. Costa Rica generates about 4,000 metric tons of solid waste each day, while only about 13% is recycled. An estimate for 2022 found that households generated more than 229,000 metric tons of plastic waste, with hundreds of tons reaching aquatic environments and tens of thousands of tons affecting land ecosystems.

For Guacalillo, that national problem becomes visible on the sand. The beach’s location makes it particularly vulnerable because it effectively sits at the end of a drainage system serving a large portion of the country’s most densely populated region. Cleaning the shoreline can improve conditions temporarily, but it does not stop more garbage from moving downstream.

That means residents and volunteers are fighting the problem at its final destination rather than at its source. Still, the community sees environmental recovery as part of Guacalillo’s economic future. The new center is intended not only to organize cleanups but also to create opportunities for local families, environmental education and sustainable tourism.

For now, volunteers continue returning to the beach, picking up bottles, plastic, shoes, syringes and countless other reminders of a pollution problem that began many kilometers upstream.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Route 32 Reopens After a Morning Landslide Shuts the Highway
World.content:
If you are driving to the Caribbean today, Route 32 is open. It was not open this morning, and the conditions that closed it have not gone anywhere. The Ministry of Public Works and Transportation shut the highway shortly after 9 a.m. this morning, when material came down onto the road. Crews cleared it and the ministry restored traffic at 1:39 p.m., about four hours later.

No reopening time was given while the road was shut. That is standard, and it is not the authorities being cagey with you. Nobody can estimate a reopening until crews reach the site, see how much material came down and confirm the slope above it has stopped moving.

If the next closure catches you, you have three ways around. Route 10, between Siquirres and Turrialba, takes any vehicle. So does the Bajos de Chilamate-Vuelta de Kooper corridor. Vara Blanca is open to light vehicles only, so leave the loaded pickup and the heavy SUV off it.

All three add real time to the trip, and all three get crowded fast when Route 32 goes down. Build in the extra hours before you leave rather than discovering them at the Zurquí backup. The reason this keeps happening sits in the terrain. Route 32 climbs through Braulio Carrillo National Park on a stretch cut between steep, forested slopes, and the ground there has been saturated for weeks.

Once soil is that wet, it stops absorbing rain and starts sliding. It does not take a downpour to bring rock, mud and whole trees onto the lanes. A moderate shower on already-soaked ground will do it.

That is exactly the pattern today. Tropical Wave No. 32 crossed the country this morning with the Intertropical Convergence Zone sitting overhead, and the Caribbean slope and Northern Zone are under a yellow alert because of it. Six-hour rainfall totals of 20 to 50 millimeters (0.8 to 2 inches) were forecast for the region, with localized peaks near 75 millimeters (3 inches) in the mountains.

So check the road right before you leave, not the night before. A highway that reopens at lunchtime can be shut again by dinner, and the status you saw yesterday tells you almost nothing about the status now.

Road updates go out on the ministry’s social media as they happen rather than on a fixed schedule, which is worth knowing if you are used to checking a website and assuming silence means the road is fine. Today’s closure also landed on a holiday. Saturday is Mother’s Day, a mandatory-pay national holiday, which puts far more cars on the road than an ordinary weekend and makes every alternate route slower than the map suggests.

This is at least the second time this month the highway has been cut. It closed on the evening of August 5 and stayed shut into the following morning, and it went down repeatedly in July during the flooding that followed Tropical Wave No. 24.

Route 32 is the only fast link between the Central Valley and Limón, and it carries commuters, tour buses and the freight moving to and from the ports at Moín. When it shuts, the cost lands on everyone at once, which is why a four-hour closure counts as a good outcome here.

Green season runs to November, and the slopes above this road will keep giving way until the ground dries out. The realistic answer is not to avoid the Caribbean but to treat the drive as something to time rather than assume.

World.title: Costa Rica Estate Becomes Refuge for Rare Agami Heron
World.content:
Around 1,000 agami herons have made a private estate in Guatuso their home, creating an unusual concentration of one of the most elusive heron species found in Costa Rica. Its near the Caño Negro wetlands, the property has become an important refuge and breeding site for the birds, prompting researchers, local residents, and the landowners to work together to study and protect the colony.

Researchers from the National Distance Education University (UNED) are monitoring the site and plan to continue carrying out censuses. Their work will focus not only on determining how many herons are present but also on counting nests and chicks to better understand the colony’s reproductive success.

The agami heron ranges from Mexico to South America but is rarely seen because of its secretive behavior and preference for densely vegetated wetland habitats. In Costa Rica, the species is primarily associated with humid areas in the Caribbean region and the Osa Peninsula.

It is also among the most colorful herons in the Neotropics. While many heron species are dominated by white, gray, brown, or dark tones, the agami heron is known for its distinctive and vibrant plumage.

Efforts to study the Guatuso colony began after the property owner contacted UNED and requested assistance in researching the birds. The owner also expressed an interest in investing resources to maintain the environmental conditions that have allowed the colony to establish itself.

The initiative has since expanded beyond scientific monitoring to include environmental education and community participation. People working on the estate are being trained to recognize threats and understand how their activities can affect the areas used by the birds for feeding, resting, and nesting.

For nearby communities, the colony could also become an opportunity to promote birdwatching and nature-based tourism in Katira, particularly because of its proximity to the Caño Negro wetlands. Community leader Odir Rojas Gómez stressed that the presence of such a large colony brings both opportunities and responsibilities.

“We want the communities to be part of its protection and for people who come to learn about it to understand that they are facing a space we must care for future generations,” he said. Researchers, however, warn that increased attention could pose risks if tourism is not carefully managed.

Herons and other waterbirds can be particularly vulnerable to disturbance during nesting periods. Visitors approaching too closely, excessive noise, or a constant human presence can cause adult birds to temporarily leave their nests, potentially exposing eggs and chicks to predators or falls.

For that reason, researchers are considering measures such as establishing minimum viewing distances, using binoculars and telescopes, and creating camouflaged observation areas. The objective is to avoid mass tourism while allowing people to experience the colony without disturbing it. “We don’t want the interest sparked by this gathering to end up becoming a threat,” said Ever Shion Salas, project designer and manager at UNED.

Continued monitoring of adults, nests, and chicks will help researchers determine how the colony develops over time and what conservation measures are necessary to protect this unusual gathering of agami herons.

World.title: Venus Williams Falls to Emiliana Arango in Cincinnati Open First Round
World.content:
Venus Williams’ return to the Cincinnati Open ended in the first round Friday as Colombian qualifier Emiliana Arango defeated the seven-time Grand Slam champion 6-2, 6-2 at the Lindner Family Tennis Center in Mason, Ohio. Arango needed just 66 minutes to eliminate the 46-year-old Williams, who entered the WTA 1000 tournament with a wild card. The loss leaves Williams still searching for her first singles victory of the 2026 season.

The match offered another reminder of how difficult Williams’ latest stretch on tour has become. She produced flashes of the aggressive tennis that made her one of the sport’s dominant players, finishing with 20 winners. But those shots were outweighed by 40 unforced errors.

Arango took a much different approach. The 25-year-old Colombian relied on her movement and consistency, committing only nine unforced errors while repeatedly forcing Williams to hit another ball. Arango finished with eight winners but rarely gave Williams the free points she needed to take control of the match.

Williams struggled particularly on serve. Arango won 60 of the 99 total points played, while Williams managed 39. The Colombian also consistently put pressure on Williams’ service games and never allowed the American to establish much momentum.

For Arango, ranked No. 95 in the world, the victory was one of the more memorable moments of her career. She was born only months after Williams won her first Grand Slam singles championship in 2000 and said afterward that facing a player she had watched growing up felt surreal. The reward for Arango is another major test. She advances to face defending Cincinnati champion Iga Swiatek in the second round.

Williams’ Cincinnati singles appearance was her latest attempt to continue a professional career that began in 1994. She owns 49 WTA singles titles, seven Grand Slam singles championships and an Olympic singles gold medal, and spent 11 weeks as the world No. 1. Before Friday’s match, she held a 12-10 career record in Cincinnati, highlighted by a semifinal appearance in 2012 and a quarterfinal run in 2019.

Despite the singles defeat, Williams’ Cincinnati Open is not necessarily over. She and younger sister Serena Williams received a wild card into the women’s doubles draw, setting up their first tournament together since the 2022 US Open. The sisters have won 14 Grand Slam doubles championships and three Olympic doubles gold medals but have never previously competed together in doubles at Cincinnati.

That reunion will now become the next focus for Venus after another difficult afternoon in singles.

World.title: The four Bedran sisters: the women behind San Ignacio Resort Hotel’s 50 years
World.content:
The four Bedran sisters: the women behind San Ignacio Resort Hotel’s 50 years

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): As San Ignacio Resort Hotel marks its 50th anniversary, the property is honouring the family that has kept the founder’s dream alive, and in particular, the four sisters who took the reins and never let go.

Behind every great legacy are those who carry it forward, the hotel wrote in its tribute, noting that for nearly five decades the Bedran family has remained at the heart of the hotel’s story.

That story begins with Escandar Bedran and his wife, who married in September 1953 and raised seven children: Mrs. Terry B. Carter, Mrs. Nazle B. Kuylen, Mrs. Mariam B. Roberson, Mr. Abdala Bedran, Mr. Escandar Bedran, Amin Bedran and Mrs. Paulita B. Figueroa. When the patriarch, who built the hotel in 1976 after fires twice destroyed his beloved Stork Club, retired in 1996, management passed to his daughters, with his encouragement to continue the legacy of what he built.

They have done exactly that. Under the family’s stewardship, the hilltop property grew into the destination known today as the only jungle in town, keeping a Belizean family name over the door through five decades when so many local institutions changed hands or disappeared.

Fifty years on, the Bedran crest still flies over the hotel, and the founder’s daughters still carry the dream forward.

World.title: Caleigh-Rose West crowned Miss Universe Belize 2026
World.content:
Caleigh-Rose West crowned Miss Universe Belize 2026

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize has a new queen. Caleigh-Rose West was crowned Miss Universe Belize 2026, the organization announced, declaring “the crown is yours” and wishing her an unforgettable journey as she prepares to represent Belize on the Miss Universe stage.

West emerged the official winner from the field of delegates at the national pageant, earning the right to carry Belize’s flag into one of the most watched competitions on the planet.

Her crowning night, however, did not pass without controversy. During a segment showcasing Belizean heritage, the stage’s digital backdrop displayed what viewers immediately identified as Tikal, the famous temple site located in Guatemala, rather than any of Belize’s own celebrated sites such as Xunantunich, Caracol or Altun Ha. The image spread quickly on social media, with critics calling it a glaring error for a national pageant and raising questions about oversight under the organization’s foreign ownership. The production decision was no fault of the delegates, and the organization had not publicly addressed the matter up to news time.

None of it diminishes West’s achievement. The new titleholder now begins the preparation road to the Miss Universe stage, where Belize’s queens have steadily raised the country’s profile.

Congratulations pour in for Caleigh-Rose West, Miss Universe Belize 2026.

World.title: Belize joins regional push to connect Central America’s trade and borders
World.content:
Belize joins regional push to connect Central America’s trade and borders

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize has taken a seat in the room where Central America’s future trade routes are being drawn. A delegation comprising Mrs. Narda Garcia, Chief Executive Officer in the Office of the Prime Minister, Investment and Civil Aviation, in her capacity as Alternate Governor to the Inter-American Development Bank, and Ms. Cinnamon Bottaro, Belize’s Representative on the IDB Board of Directors, participated in the Ministerial Dialogue “Central America at the Center: Connectivity and Integration for a more Competitive Region” in Panama City on August 12.

The gathering, part of the IDB’s América en el Centro initiative covering Central America, Panama and the Dominican Republic, brought together ministers of finance, transport and trade to work on practical solutions: improving regional roads and border crossings, modernizing customs and logistics, mobilizing investment and easing the movement of goods.

Discussions included Cargo Pass, an initiative to move cargo across borders safely, efficiently and with greater traceability, exactly the kind of system that will determine how quickly and cheaply Belizean exports reach regional markets.

Government says Belize’s participation ensures the country is part of the planning from the outset, because the infrastructure and trade systems designed today will shape regional commerce for decades. As the only nation holding membership in both SICA and CARICOM, Belize sees an opportunity not simply to connect with its neighbours, but to help connect Central America with Mexico and the Caribbean.

World.title: New flights, quiet season, free night: the case for Las Terrazas this fall
World.content:
New flights, quiet season, free night: the case for Las Terrazas this fall

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize’s fall travel season is arriving with unusual momentum, and Las Terrazas Resort and Residences on Ambergris Caye sits squarely in its path.

The momentum starts in the sky. BermudAir is launching seasonal nonstop flights to Belize City from five US airports, Boston, Raleigh-Durham, Fort Lauderdale, Orlando-Sanford and Tampa Bay’s St. Petersburg-Clearwater, with fares from US$164 and the Fort Lauderdale route beginning October 26, right as fall settles in. The airline says these will be the only nonstops from all five cities, cutting layovers out of the Belize trip for whole new markets.

On the ground, fall remains the connoisseur’s season: calmer beaches, easier tables, softer rates, and a reef every bit as brilliant as in the winter crush. Las Terrazas, the beachfront member of the L.V.X Collection of Preferred Hotels and Resorts north of San Pedro, pairs that quiet with oceanfront residences, dining, a spa and the reef at its dock.

The final piece is the math: the resort’s stay four nights, get the fifth free offer runs through December 15, stretching every fall booking an extra day.

New routes in the air, an island exhaling below, and a free night waiting. Bookings at www.lasterrazasresort.com or via WhatsApp through the Las Terrazas Resort and Residences Facebook page.

World.title: Leader of the Opposition hails people power after Speednet deal is stopped
World.content:
Leader of the Opposition hails people power after Speednet deal is stopped

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Leader of the Opposition Tracy Taegar Panton has issued a Sunday message celebrating what she calls a strong wave of civic engagement across the nation, days after Cabinet withdrew support for BTL’s proposed acquisition of Speednet.

“Your voice matters. Speaking truth to power matters. How our country is governed matters,” the Albert area representative wrote, giving thanks for “every Belizean who has risked so much to speak out, stand up, and to actively champion a more productive Belize.”

Panton’s honour roll named the coalition that stood against the deal: the BCCI, the NTUCB and its Governing Council, the NGOs, NEAB, the Council of Churches, members of the independent media, “our great United Democratic Party,” and every citizen who raised concerns on social media or peacefully protested. “We See You. We Hear You. We Appreciate You,” she wrote.

The opposition leader then turned the moment forward. “Corruption and the abuse of public office remain serious concerns,” she charged, calling on Belizeans to remain informed, vigilant and engaged, and to press for transparency, accountability and good governance “until those responsible are held to account.”

“We should never underestimate the power of an engaged citizenry,” Panton wrote. “We maintain that power belongs in the hands of the people.”

The message closed with Sunday blessings for the nation, signed One Love.

World.title: Woman bolts from station after cuffs are loosened, caught two weeks later
World.content:
Woman bolts from station after cuffs are loosened, caught two weeks later

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Bella Vista Village woman who bolted from a police station moments after an officer kindly loosened her handcuffs has been recaptured two weeks later, spotted at a village bar, and formally charged with escaping from lawful custody.

According to the Belize Police Department, on Saturday, August 1, 2026, at about 6:40 p.m., the woman was in custody at the Bella Vista Police Sub Station for possession of a controlled drug and possession of a pipe, with charges yet to be laid.

She was in handcuffs but complained they were too tight, and an officer loosened them. Because the cell block was full, holding only male occupants at the time, she was placed on a seat while another officer prepared her custody record and acknowledgement form.

That was when she made her move, running out of the police station. Officers pursued, but the chase proved fruitless as she fled through the bushes.

The trail stayed quiet for nearly two weeks. Then, on Friday, August 14, an officer saw the woman at a bar in Bella Vista Village, where she was apprehended, detained, and escorted back to the very station she had fled.

On Saturday, August 15, at 6:30 a.m., police formally arrested and charged Riccy Bonilla, a 32-year-old unemployed woman of Bella Vista Village, with the offence of escaping from lawful custody.

World.title: Teen escapes police mobile and takes the corporal’s handcuffs with him
World.content:
Teen escapes police mobile and takes the corporal’s handcuffs with him

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 17-year-old wanted for theft escaped from a police vehicle in Bella Vista Village while still wearing an officer’s handcuffs, only to be recaptured at his own residence the next morning, without the handcuffs, which he could not account for. He has now been formally charged with theft and escaping from lawful custody.

According to the Belize Police Department, on Thursday, August 13, 2026, at about 5:35 p.m., officers on mobile patrol in Bella Vista spotted a male person known to be wanted by police for the crime of theft. Officers approached him, informed him of the report against him, cautioned him, and placed him under arrest.

What followed was proper juvenile procedure. Because the detainee is still a minor, officers escorted him to his mother’s residence so she could accompany her son to the police station, as the law requires a parent or guardian’s presence for a minor in custody.

The procedure created the opening. While at his mother’s residence, the teen jumped out of the police mobile and made good his escape, taking the corporal’s handcuffs with him. Efforts to recapture him at the time proved fruitless.

His freedom lasted one night. On Friday, August 14, at about 10:00 a.m., police recaptured the teen at his residence. Upon recapture, officers noted the handcuffs were no longer on his person, and when asked about them, he could give no account of the cuffs. He was informed he would be charged with theft and escaping from lawful custody, detained, and escorted to the Bella Vista Police Station.

At the station, the juvenile safeguards resumed: he was issued an acknowledgement form, which he signed, with his mother signing as witness.

On Saturday, August 15, police formally arrested and charged the 17-year-old labourer of Bella Vista with the crimes of theft and escaping from lawful custody. As he is a minor, his identity is being withheld, and as with any matter before the court, he is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty.

World.title: A golden Sunday before Monday turns wet again
World.content:
A golden Sunday before Monday turns wet again

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The weekend closes exactly as forecast, under mainly fair skies with sunshine and the familiar 95-degree inland heat, but the reprieve is short: showers and thunderstorms build back across the country from late Monday morning, with periods of rain over most areas, especially the coast, by Monday night.

According to the National Meteorological Service, mainly fair weather conditions prevail. Skies will be sunny with a few cloudy spells today and partly cloudy tonight. Showers or thunderstorms will be isolated, with a low chance of a few more over southern and some coastal areas later this morning or early afternoon.

Temperatures along the coast will reach a high of 89 degrees Fahrenheit (32 Celsius) and a low of 81 (27 Celsius). Inland areas will be the hottest, climbing to 95 degrees Fahrenheit (35 Celsius) before dropping to 74 (23 Celsius). In the hills, expect a high of 83 degrees Fahrenheit (28 Celsius) and a low of 68 (20 Celsius). With the mercury back at 95, the Sunday rules apply: water close, shade often.

At sea, conditions run choppy, with east to northeast winds of 5 to 15 knots and waves of 3 to 5 feet, workable water for the weekend’s final runs with the usual care on smaller craft.

On the tropical front, the calm holds. Tropical cyclone formation is not expected over the region during the next 48 hours.

Looking ahead to Monday and Monday night, skies turn cloudy at times, with showers and thunderstorms isolated at first, then gradually increasing around the country from late Monday morning or afternoon. Some showers, thunderstorms, and periods of rain are possible over most areas, especially the coast, Monday night, a forecast worth watching for anyone with Tuesday plans in Belmopan or Belize City.

Today’s low tides are at 6:34 AM and 6:44 PM, with a high tide at 12:29 PM and another high at 12:36 AM tomorrow. The sun rose at 5:35 AM and will set at 6:17 PM. The forecast was issued by forecaster Tareek Matthews.

World.title: Franno’s last lap
World.content:
Paul Francis (left) prepares to take the urn with the cremains of his brother, legendary Jamaican track and field coach Stephen Francis, down the red-carpeted track as Sport Minister Olivia “Babsy” Grange (right) and Olympian Asafa Powell (second right) stand with athletes forming a guard of honour at the end of the thanksgiving service for Stephen Francis’s life at National Indoor Sports Centre in St Andrew on Saturday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)Photo: Garfield Robinson

HE spent a lifetime on the sidelines, stopwatch and clipboard in hand, watching athletes take their places on the track, but at the thanksgiving service for his life on Saturday, Vincent Stephen “Franno” Francis was in the spotlight. He made his final lap down a red-carpeted track, his cremains carried in a platinum urn as athletes he had trained and mentored formed a guard of honour — a fitting tribute for the legendary Jamaican track and field coach who produced world beaters.

The emotion was unmistakable as athletes fought back tears while ushering Francis out of the National Indoor Sports Centre, a stone’s throw from the National Stadium where many of them had delivered some of their greatest performances. This time, however, there was no race to prepare for, no stopwatch to start, and no final instructions to give, only the painful realisation that they were saying goodbye to the coach who had spent a lifetime helping them find their way to the finish line, and now they were returning the favour.

For approximately five minutes, sprint legends Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce, Shericka Jackson, Kishane Thompson, Elaine Thompson Herah, and many more who spent years being taught the art and science of sprinting stood still as family members, friends, Government officials, and colleagues looked on, reminiscing on the life of a world-class coach.

A nod to his alma mater, Wolmer’s Boys’ School, the sports centre and many attendees were decked in maroon and gold for the four-hour-long service that was enveloped in an atmosphere that swung from grief to celebration.

Pot covers echoed during tributes about Francis’s excellent track record, tears flowed when travelling down memory lane, laughter filled the room at comical moments, and musical tributes and selections provided much-needed comfort.

In his tribute, delivered by Finance Minister Fayval Williams, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness praised Francis for demonstrating what was possible when natural talent was matched with world-class coaching, structure, and preparation. He noted that, through the formation of the Maximising Velocity and Power (MVP) Track Club, Francis helped create a pathway for Jamaican athletes to develop at home, at a time when many were leaving the island in search of training opportunities abroad.

“Athletes under his guidance became Olympic and World champions, record holders and household names. Yet his influence cannot be measured by counting medals alone. He developed people, he established standards, and he challenged athletes to become more disciplined, more prepared, and more demanding of themselves,” wrote Holness.

“He also helped prove that a Jamaican coaching programme could consistently produce performances of the highest international standard. In that sense, his impact reached well beyond MVP. He contributed to the evolution of the Jamaican coaching profession and to a stronger national system of athlete development,” he said.

It was for these reasons that Sports Minister Olivia Grange urged the congregation not to mourn, but to celebrate the man who possessed an extraordinary vision backed by purpose and confidence that what he was doing would bring the results that he envisioned.

“Francis understood that talent was only the beginning. Talent had to be developed, potential had to be channelled, and dreams had to be matched by commitment. That philosophy, my brothers and sisters, helped to shape athletes and contributed significantly to Jamaica’s remarkable place in world athletics. Francis possessed technical mastery. He studied speed like a scientist. Above all, he had a strong belief in Jamaica and the potential of our people,” said Grange.

She added that to honour his legacy, the Government is in discussions to provide student-athletes at the University of Technology, Jamaica, the home of the MVP track club, a scholarship in his name.

The move was welcomed by president of the university Dr Kevin Brown, who thanked Francis for choosing the campus as his training ground and placing the institution on the map, one athlete at a time. He remembered Francis for his bluntness, discipline, and belief in the potential of Jamaica, joking that he never wasted words and advocated fiercely for his athletes.

An emotional Brigitte Foster-Hylton and Asafa Powell, two sprint legends who reaped the rewards of Francis’s brilliance, stood as living evidence of his legacy, though struggling to steady their voices as they fought back tears. Between the emotion, they recalled cherished memories, from dodging train conductors in Italy to travelling in Francis’s old car, thanking the coach who had taken a chance on them, believed in their potential, and pushed them towards global success.

“Everything I became started with one man who saw something in a young man before anyone else did,” said Powell, Foster-Hylton finishing his speech as he broke down in tears.

She thanked Francis for every lesson, sacrifice, laugh, and opportunity, noting that he did not just change her life, he changed countless lives.

“Rest well, Franno. Your whistle might be silent, but your legacy lives on,” she said through tears.

Eulogised by his brother, Paul, who also spoke through shaky breaths, the decorated coach was remembered as a friend, a loyalist, a protector of his athletes, a family man, and a coach.

Adrian Laidlaw wiped away tears as he declared that delivering a tribute to his best friend was the hardest job he was ever tasked with. He said when Francis closed his eyes on July 4, 2026, a piece of Jamaica left with him, and his legacy will always be remembered.

Recounting cherished memories of a man he described as both mentor and friend, MVP President Bruce James said Francis made countless sacrifices in his mission to put Jamaica firmly on the international athletics stage, remaining committed to the vision even in the face of doubt.

James recalled that Francis’s dedication to his athletes never wavered, even from his hospital bed, where he continued asking for updates on their progress — a final testament to a coach whose commitment to his craft and athletes endured to the very end.

“History has proven you right, Franno. The World records, the Olympic records, the World champions, the Olympic champions, the world athletes of the year, the numerous athletes who won medals on the global stage achieved more than they ever thought possible and became better versions of themselves because they were a part of MVP,” said James in a written tribute.

World.title: KFC eats into jerk sales
World.content:
Morant Bay jerk pork vendor Johnny sharing his experience since KFC set up shop in the St Thomas capital town late last year. He told the Observer that before KFC opened its doors he would prepare some 30 pounds of pork each day and most times it would “sell out”. Now he prepares about 20 pounds of pork daily and even that amount is not always completely sold. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

TRADITIONAL jerk vendors in Morant Bay, St Thomas, are reporting a decline in their business since fast food giant KFC officially opened its historic first restaurant in the parish in January this year.

But the vendors say while sales are down they are not being squeezed out of the business which, for years, has attracted residents of the parish as well as scores of people passing through the town.

One jerk pork vendor, who gave his name only as Johnny, last Thursday told the Jamaica Observer that while his business remains open, “it’s not as warm as it once was”.

Johnny, who also works as a butcher, said the business has slowed down and the increase in sales he normally sees during holiday periods did not materialise this year.

He told the Sunday Observer that before KFC opened its doors he would prepare some 30 pounds of pork each day and most times it would “sell out”.

According to Johnny, he now prepares about 20 pounds of pork daily and even that amount is not always completely sold.

He pointed out that even his children sometimes ask for chicken from KFC.

“So I have to go in there and spend to buy what they want,” said Johnny, who added that he continues to receive support from loyal customers who prefer his jerked pork.

Another jerk vendor, who requested anonymity, said the arrival of KFC would naturally result in some loss of business for local food operators, but he does not believe it poses a major threat.

“I don’t know, it would be a downgrade in a sense because most people gravitate towards the KFC and dem business deh,” the vendor said as he told the Sunday Observer that there had been “a slight drop-off” in his business since KFC opened.

“It’s gradually going down, but sometimes it’s up again,” the vendor said, even as he underscored that he welcomes the presence of the immensely popular KFC.

He pointed to the demand for employment opportunities and development in the parish, and described KFC’s arrival as a positive development for the integrated industrial and commercial complex dubbed the Morant Bay Urban Centre.

“People need jobs as well, so I would say it’s a good thing,” the vendor said.

KFC invested $350 million to establish its Morant Bay restaurant which provides jobs for more than 50 people.

The store was warmly received by several residents of St Thomas with one person describing the opening as “a wonderful and historic moment for the parish”.

At the official opening in January, Mark Myers, managing director of Restaurants of Jamaica — the operators of the KFC franchise locally — said the decision to locate in Morant Bay was deliberate and rooted in confidence in the area’s potential.

“This opening is about more than adding another restaurant to the network. It reflects a deliberate decision to invest in communities beyond Kingston and to grow in places where opportunity and potential continue to emerge.

“When plans for the Morant Bay Urban Centre were first taking shape we saw an opportunity to be part of something transformational. We want to participate in the continued development of this parish, to invest early and to grow alongside the community — [and] that conviction is what brought us here,” Myers said then.

World.title: Vision. Mission. Spirit. Impact
World.content:
Djimon Hounsou.

The fourth annual Screenwriters’ Workshop hosted by Strike Star Entertainment is set to take place over two days from September 15-16 at Edna Manley College of the Visual and Performing Arts.

The workshop, which is designed to introduce young and aspiring professionals to the film industry, will feature a keynote address by respected American film director Benny Boom.

Other presenters and panellists include Vanessa Ballesteros (television producer and showrunner); actor John Chambers; producer, writer and executive Marvin Peart; Soyini Chang, entrepreneur, strategist, and creative executive; Morris Sinclair, cultural entrepreneur and project strategist; screenwriter Tyrone Rashard; John Buffalo Mailer, producer, screenwriter, journalist and playwright; Bryce Wilson, formerly of the music duo Groove Theory and a creative director, actor and producer; actor Djimon Hounsou; editor Olivia Rutigliano; and Cess Silvera, director, producer and screenwriter.

In an interview with the Jamaica Observer, Ricky Lee, CEO and founder of Strike Star Entertainment, explained why he decided to host the screenwriter workshop in Jamaica.

“I’ve always believed Jamaica has one of the richest storytelling cultures in the world. The creative energy here is raw, honest, and deeply rooted in lived experience. When Paul Eckstein [American actor, television writer and producer] passed, I felt an even stronger pull to continue the work he inspired — creating spaces where emerging writers can grow, be seen, and be supported. Edna Manley College represents that same spirit of artistic discipline and cultural pride. Hosting the workshop here allows us to honour Paul’s legacy while investing directly in Jamaica’s next generation of storytellers,” said Lee.

The very first workshop was held at The Mico University College, which Lee shared was a deeply meaningful beginning.

“Our partner Steven Golding teaches at Mico, and he helped connect us to the institution. Mico is one of Jamaica’s first teachers’ colleges, so starting there felt aligned with Paul’s belief in education, access, and community. That foundation continues to guide everything we do,” explained Lee.

He told the Observer that the objective behind the workshop is to expand creative minds and opportunities.

“Over two days, participants learn the fundamentals of screenwriting, story structure, character development, and the business of film. We focus on mentorship, industry exposure, and building confidence; the same values Paul championed throughout his career. We’re targeting emerging and aspiring screenwriters — young creatives, students, and anyone who feels called to write for film or television. You don’t need industry experience; you just need imagination, commitment, and a desire to grow,” said Lee.

Interested participants can visit Strike Star Entertainment online and register.

“Jamaica has extraordinary talent,” opined Lee, “what’s often missing is access, mentorship, and industry level exposure… By bringing global professionals directly to Jamaican creatives we’re strengthening the foundation of the country’s emerging film ecosystem. And in many ways, we’re continuing the work Paul believed in: Empowering storytellers and expanding opportunity,” he said.

Benny Boom, who directed the music video for Sean Paul’s Like Glue as well as videos for several acts, including Busta Rhymes, Nas, Nelly, LL Cool J, Nicki Minaj, Akon, 50 Cent, and GloRilla, is best known for directing the 2017 Tupak Shakur biopic All Eyez on Me.

He told the Observer what participants attending the workshop can expect.

“I’m bringing my experience, my perspective, and my commitment to helping writers understand how powerful their voice is. Paul Eckstein was someone I deeply respected; not just for his creativity, but for the way he championed storytellers. His belief in developing writers and expanding access is something I carry with me. So, when I step into this workshop, I’m bringing that same spirit — honesty, mentorship, and a real desire to help emerging writers elevate their craft,” said Benny Boom. “You can expect clarity and real, practical guidance. I want writers to understand how directors read scripts, how we translate words into images, and what makes a story visually compelling. I want participants to walk away with tools they can use immediately.”

According to Benny Boom, he couldn’t turn down the offer to be a part of the workshop.

“I said yes right away. Ricky shared the vision, and he shared Paul’s influence on this workshop. Paul was someone whose work and creative energy I admired, so being part of something inspired by him felt meaningful. Coming back for a second year was an easy decision, this workshop is doing real work for Jamaican creatives, and I’m proud to support it,” said the respected director.

World.title: Fears flow in St Thomas
World.content:
Resident Charline Gabas stands in front her home and points to the dirt pushed along the edge of the path where the Plantain Garden River flows in Bath, St Thomas, last Thursday.Photos: Karl Mclarty

JUST over nine months after Hurricane Melissa sent residents of Bath, St Thomas, scrambling from their houses as the Plantain Garden River tore into its banks, washed away a parked car, and threatened to swallow lands inches from their homes, residents say a recent riverbank intervention has done little to ease their fears.

Dirt pushed along the edge in July has provided some protection, residents acknowledge, but they insist it is no substitute for a groyne in and the proper channelling of the river.

Therefore, they are warning that another bout of heavy rain could once again send floodwaters towards their homes, further eroding the riverbank and putting the wider community, including Bath Primary School, at risk.

They are also adamant that another major weather event, similar to Hurricane Melissa which ravaged sections of the island on October 28, 2025, could finally cause their homes to collapse into the river’s path.

When the Jamaica Observer returned to the area last Thursday the scene was markedly different from the one residents had confronted during Melissa’s onslaught last year.

Dirt had been pushed along the edge of the area where the riverbank had broken away, while additional dirt had been placed in the space through which the river flows, apparently to obstruct the water’s path and keep it from pushing towards the vulnerable section.

But for residents who have spent years watching the river steadily eat away at the landscape, the intervention has brought only limited reassurance.

Charline Gabas, who lives in the community at the very edge, acknowledged that the dirt has made the immediate area feel somewhat safer, but said it has not addressed what she considers the fundamental problem — the absence of a proper channel to carry the river away from the homes.

“Don’t get me wrong, enuh, if this was not here I would not be able to stand up here, cause when mi stand up here suh it is a little bit safer. But listen, what we are saying — because we have been here for years — they need to take out that piece and channel it to that dry piece of land over the other side, dig it and carry down there suh so [that] when the river comes down it goes that side and follows that channel instead of come over here. Because with how it stay now, the water is going to come over her same way,” Gabas told the Jamaica Observer.

Last October, as Hurricane Melissa battered Jamaica, sections of the Plantain Garden River bank collapsed, prompting residents living nearby to quickly evacuate their homes. Video footage circulated on social media showed residents fleeing as a section of the riverbank gave way, sweeping away a parked car in the process.

For residents, the episode was not entirely unexpected.

During an October visit, Bath resident Theodore Bailey said the community had been calling for the river to be properly protected for more than two decades. He pointed to cracks in the soil near the threatened homes and warned that the saturated ground could still give way even after the hurricane had passed.

Furthermore, the river’s movement has also changed the landscape over time, according to Gabas who rejected the suggestion that residents had simply built their homes too close to the river’s path.

She said the river was once much farther from the houses and that the encroachment had occurred gradually, as the water continued to wash away the land.

“We could not see river and build we house beside it, we are not that stupid… That is what I am trying to tell people, that the river was all the way over there suh but over time it keep on coming over and washing away the land,” she said, noting that she has lived in the community for 19 years and has watched the river steadily encroach on the land.

Initially, residents had suggested that large boulders be used to strengthen the vulnerable section, similar to measures they had seen elsewhere.

But Gabas said the current deterioration of the riverbank means that approach is no longer enough.

“At the time we ask them fi turn the river and we did a seh get the big stone dem, at that time it never suh bad suh we did a suggest they could use the boulders like wah dem use over Yallahs or Port Royal road [Palisadoes]. But then it get so bad now so that is no longer an option. The river have to groyne back, turn the river and groyne it back,” Gabas said.

Tracy-Ann Emanuel, another Bath resident, said the current intervention does not appear capable of withstanding the force of the river during sustained rainfall. She argued that the river needs to be properly trained — a process that, in practical terms, involves controlling and directing the water’s course so that it does not continue spilling into vulnerable areas.

“Well this nuh mek any sense. They need to rebuild a groyne, this place really need fi groyne back, because if one next big shower of rain come we are going to be in problem, so when PG [Plantain Garden] river a come it a guh push back the dirt fi come over here suh,” she reasoned.

Concerns were also raised about how long it took officials to address the issue. According to Gabas, the work was carried out roughly three to four weeks before the Sunday Observer revisited the area last Thursday.

She said residents had become increasingly concerned as the hurricane season progressed and they saw no work being done yet were given no explanation about who was responsible for the eventual intervention.

She said the lack of consultation has added to the frustration.

According to Gabas, workers arrived, carried out the work, and left without explaining to residents what was being done or what the intervention was intended to achieve. At the time of the Sunday Observer’s visit she said residents did not know which agency had undertaken the work.

Gabas said residents are particularly anxious because relocating is not a realistic option for many of them.

“We cannot move, we nuh have any options. When hurricane came October and we had to move out we things because of what happened and by November I had to move in again [that was one thing], but [now] mi nuh have a next option. Mi nuh have the money to buy land and start over and make a next house again,” she said.

So residents are watching the weather closely and worrying about what another prolonged period of rainfall could bring.

Gabas said the dirt has at least created enough of a barrier to make it possible for her to stand at the edge of the vulnerable area without feeling as exposed as before. But she does not regard that as evidence that the underlying danger has been addressed.

She also pointed to what she sees as a gap between the authorities carrying out physical work and the residents living with the consequences.

Gabas said the Sunday Observer team was the first group, since Hurricane Melissa, to return and speak directly with residents about the condition of the river and their concerns.

“From Hurricane Melissa come last year October unnu a the first set of people who come and have a conversation with we and ask we about the river, nobody else. Anybody else we see, dem just come work and point; dem nuh know we and we nuh know dem. The tractor man seh a work him get fi push dirt and him just a work! The rest a people dem just come in and look, and point finger, and gwaan,” she expressed.

The National Works Agency (NWA) has since been identified as the agency responsible for the intervention work.

Stephen Shaw, the NWA’s manager of communication and customer services, confirmed to the Sunday Observer last Friday that the agency carried out the intervention but said he could not provide details at the time.

For the residents of Bath, however, the immediate concern is less about who moved the dirt and more about whether it will hold when the river next rises.

World.title: RESPECT, FRANNO
World.content:
Racers Track Club Head Coach Glen Mills in attendance at the thanksgiving service for the life of the late MVP Track Club head Coach Stephen Francis at the National Indoor Sports Centre on Saturday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

ON Saturday the National Indoor Sports Centre (NISC) didn’t echo with starting guns. It echoed with choir voices, applause, and songs.

At centre court — usually the home to the Sunshine Girls — there was no casket. However, on a podium marked 1st, 2nd and 3rd — There was only one thing: the urn of Coach Stephen “Franno” Francis.

Hundreds filled the arena, waitng in silence as a photo of Francis on a large screen overlooked over the proceedings.

The University of Technology, Jamaica Choir opened the thanksgiving service with All creatures of our God and King as urn bearers Pearnel Charles and Gloria Charles led the procession.

Sport Minister Olivia Grange delivered the Government’s tribute to the man who built Jamaica’s sprint dynasty.

“Stephen Francis was a legendary athletics coach and more. He was a mentor, a teacher, a colleague, a friend, and sometimes, perhaps, a very demanding voice reminding you that you could do better,” Grange said.

“He believed in hard work. He believed in discipline. He believed in preparation. And, above all, he believed in the potential of people. Above all, he had a strong belief in Jamaica and the potential of our people.

“He proved we did not need an overseas college or camp to run 9.7 seconds. What was needed was discipline and a good coach who would not accept ‘good enough’. We go above gold — a platinum medal [is deserved]for your life’s work, Franno. Rest in peace, ‘Big Coach’.”

The outpouring of respect and love for Francis, which everyone spoke about, was evident as long before the scheduled time of 11:00 am for the start of the service family, friends and well-wishers began to descend on the NISC to pay their final farewell to the legend.

Olympic and World 100m hurdles champion Brigitte Foster-Hylton traced MVP Track and Field Club’s (MVP) beginning to 1999.

“I first met Stephen Francis in the summer of 1999… he told me that he thought I had world-class potential but it would take some work. It was after that meeting the club MVP had its first athlete,” she said.

“Franno was my coach, my physio, my support psychologist — everything. Being on the European cicuit alone without a coach, I had lost two consecutive races to Gail Devers of the USA and I had to race her for a third time. Franno was watching the races from home and he picked up the phone and called Patrick [Foster-Hylton’s husband] and told him to borrow $2,000 and go to the race because I am going to beat Gail. And guess what, I won the race,” Foster-Hylton said.

Former 100m World record holder Asafa Powell stood to speak not as an Olympian, but as a son.

“Today, I’m not here as a former world record holder, or an Olympian. I’m standing here as that little country boy whose life was changed by one man,” Powell said.

He remembered in 2001, Boys’ and Girls’ Champs a false start, and a disqualification with no future in mind.

“Then one day, Paul Francis showed up at my school… He asked if I would want to come to UTech. Truth is, I had no idea what UTech was. My parents left the decision to my brother Nigel and me, and we took the chance. That decision led me to Coach Stephen Francis, and from the moment I met him my life changed forever,” Powell remembered.

The conditions were rough.

“When my father took me to the track house the conditions weren’t great… But what kept me there wasn’t the building. It was the family coach created. Coach became more than a coach. He was another father,” Powell said.

He remembered topping up the transmission oil in Franno’s leaking Proton Saga daily.

“It seemed like a small thing back then, but now it feels priceless.”

Powell said Franno was a seer.

“I remember one day he said, ‘You’re going to break the world record, you know,’ and I laughed. Honestly, I thought he believed in me more than I believed in myself. Years later, when I broke the world record in Athens, I remembered that conversation. He wasn’t dreaming, he was seeing,” Powell said with emotion as his voice broke.

Powell said that Francis was funny. He recalled an event in Italy with no train tickets, and an inspector coming.

“Coach told us, ‘Don’t say a word. I’ll handle it.’ The officer came around and spoke Italian… Coach shook his head. The officer said ‘Speak German or Dutch’, coach said no. The officer then said ‘Speak English?’ Coach looked at the man and said, ‘No language.’ We could barely hold our laughter in. It was that moment I’ll miss the most,” Powell said as the audience broke into laughter.

“Not just the medals or the records, but those simple moments that became unforgettable,” Powell added, before breaking down in tears.

Foster-Hylton had to finish Powell’s speech.

MVP Track Club President Bruce James delivered the remembrance of Francis’s final months.

“Franno and the team had just returned to Jamaica from the World Athletics Indoor Championships in Poland. They left Poland on March 23, except he was sick. Franno was too sick, [so mush so] that he could not make it to training,” James said.

“After a week of missing training Franno called me and said that he was calling because he was too sick to drive but he wanted me to arrange a driver to take him to training in the morning, leave him, and carry him back after the afternoon session. Too sick to drive but he wanted to get to training by any means necessary,” James said.

James said that it was his time to tell the ‘big man’ no.

“I did not arrange the drive but I did send the doctor to his home. Sadly, Franno continued to decline and the only option for him was to be hospitalised,” said James.

The eulogy was delivered by Francis’s brother, Paul Francis.

Five-time Olympic gold medallist Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce read Ecclesiastes 3:1-13, “To everything there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.”

Throughout the service attendees clapped, cheered, and sang.

No race was run on Saturday but the standard Francis demanded was still there.

World.title: SUZANNE MCFAYDEN’S THIRD ACT
World.content:
Suzanne McFayden is pictured on a staircase designed by Paul Lamb. (Photo: Douglas Friedman)

“This is my third act,” says Jamaican-born writer, philanthropist, and prolific contemporary art collector Suzanne McFayden. With her youngest child graduating from college this past spring, the Jamaican-born empty nester was ready for change — and a home that reflected who she is now. The

Style Observer was only too happy to feature her 2019 stunning property in our September 2020 issue and was naturally eager to get in on the third act which saw McFayden reuniting with architect Paul Lamb (@paullambarchitects) and interior designer Jennifer Vaughn Miller

(@vaughnmillerstudio).

Tranquil reflection redefined her idea of home. After selling her 7,000-square-foot Brutalist concrete house in Austin, Texas — featured by Architectural Digest in 2019 — McFayden sought “something cosy and nourishing”, she says, “with wall space for art”. She found her “sleeping beauty” tucked into a verdant thicket of Red Oak and Live Oak trees in Austin’s Hill Country. To bring the project to life, she reunited with local architect Paul Lamb and New York City–based interior designer Jennifer Vaughn Miller, the team behind her previous industrial monolith. The result is a deeply personal Austin retreat where every room tells a story.

CREDITS

Feature by Punch Hutton

Photography by Douglas Friedman

Architect: Paul Lamb

Interior designer: Jennifer Vaughn Miller

World.title: NOT TRUE!
World.content:
ANDERSON... perhaps the most serious wound is the suggestion that panels of the court have been constituted or altered in order to secure a particular outcome in a case

Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ) President Justice Winston Anderson on Friday broke his silence on allegations surrounding his leadership of the regional body, describing as “entirely unfounded and untrue” suggestions that he interfered with the composition of panels and sought to influence judgments.

At the same time he characterised the disclosure of a series of e-mail between himself and colleague judges to the

Sunday Express newspaper in Trinidad and Tobago “as the most troubling aspect of this entire episode”, and condemned, “in the strongest possible terms, the unauthorised disclosure and publication of confidential material relating to the internal deliberations and confidential correspondence of the court”.

According to Justice Anderson, “such disclosures and their publication are wholly unacceptable and strike at one of the fundamental principles upon which every independent judiciary depends”.

“It erodes trust in the sanctity of judicial deliberations and judicial collegiality. It erodes public trust and confidence in the Third Branch, and it does untold harm to the people we are sworn to serve and betrays the trust and confidence placed in us,” the CCJ president stated.

The Sunday Express had reported that in the e-mail exchanges, a majority of the judges accused Justice Anderson of governing the regional court in an “authoritarian” and “dictatorial” manner.

The complaints, as reported by the newspaper, range from accusations of Justice Anderson unilaterally imposing a judicial dress code to allegations of “panel fixing” and attempts to influence the outcome of cases.

Addressing the allegations further, Justice Anderson said, “Perhaps the most serious wound is the suggestion that panels of the court have been constituted or altered in order to secure a particular outcome in a case.

“Such an allegation strikes at the very heart of judicial independence and public confidence in the administration of justice. It therefore warrants a clear and direct response. The allegation is wholly untrue. No judge of this court can or should be restrained from expressing his or her judicial views, or from deciding any matter according to his or her independent assessment of the law and the evidence,” Justice Anderson stated.

He said that it was “with particular concern” that he “noted suggestions in the public domain” that he has sought to influence the outcome of cases before the court.

“Those allegations are entirely unfounded and untrue,” Justice Anderson declared while explaining that a little known fact is that, “in the original jurisdiction of the court, no dissenting judgments are published”. However, the CCJ president maintained that, “the principle of unanimity is a standard practice in international courts exercising jurisdiction of this type”.

“The suggestion that judicial views were suppressed, or that any judge was directed to reach a particular conclusion, is therefore wholly without foundation. Throughout my judicial career, both as a judge and now as president, I have regarded judicial independence as inviolable. It is a principle that I have consistently defended and will continue to defend,” Justice Anderson said.

Detailing the constitution of panels within the court, the CCJ president pointed out that “the inferential leap required to elevate the issue of Bench attire to an allegation of panel-fixing is irresponsible, intellectually dishonest, injudicious and, quite simply, malevolent!”

“Accordingly, I reject entirely the suggestion that panels of this court have been constituted or altered to secure predetermined outcomes. Such allegations are unsupported by the facts, inconsistent with the court’s long-established practices, and contrary to the principles upon which this court has operated since its establishment,” Justice Anderson stated.

He however said, in putting that matter to rest going forward, “every judge of the court will be required to sit on every panel, unless the judge opts out for a legitimate reason and is excused”.

Responding to reports that he had taken a high-handed approach in deciding on the judicial dress code, the CCJ president provided the background to that development. He conceded that while he “may have approached the matter of the handling of the issue of the dress code too strongly”, he did so because he “regarded it as an institutional issue concerning the appearance, consistency and tone of the court, rather than a question directed at any individual judge”.

Said Justice Anderson: “The CCJ is the apex court for a diverse Caribbean region and population. Dress codes set by the CCJ will have implications for all courts of member states as well as for the region. The idea of individual judges adopting their own interpretation of national or traditional dress would seem to be at odds with the very concept of a Caribbean court.”

He added that “if it is the view of the region that national dress is appropriate for judges to wear on the Bench, the inevitable question of what is ‘national dress’ in a Caribbean context of diversity must be determined”.

“This must be determined by the people of the region and toward this end I propose to engage all national courts in this consultation,” Justice Anderson said further.

Addressing commentary about his meetings and discussions with the president and leader of the Opposition of Guyana regarding the prolonged acting appointments of the chancellor and chief justice of that country, Justice Anderson made it clear that he had “no personal interest or preference in who is appointed” to both positions.

“My concern has always and only been confined to the constitutional principle that the judiciary should be headed by substantively appointed office holders enjoying the full constitutional protections intended by the framers of the constitution,” Justice Anderson insisted. He said while in retrospect he believed “another course would have been much better” his actions were fed only by his concern about “the preservation of judicial independence and the constitutional integrity of the Guyanese judiciary”.

“Those considerations alone informed my actions and comments. They were not motivated by any political or other preference, personal interest, or any desire to intervene in the domestic affairs of Guyana beyond what I regarded as my responsibility as president of the final appellate court for that jurisdiction to ensure constitutional protection of the judiciary,” Justice Anderson said.

On Wednesday, the heads of judiciary of Barbados, The Bahamas, Belize, Guyana, the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court, Jamaica, and Trinidad and Tobago — which subscribe to the original and/or appellate jurisdictions of the CCJ — in a media release said, while they “do not consider it appropriate to comment upon the merits of statements or allegations attributed to individual judges, nor upon matters arising within the internal deliberative or administrative processes of the court”, they were gravely concerned “about the breach of confidentiality which resulted in the disclosure of what appear to be internal communications”.

Said the heads of the judiciary: “We remain confident in the Caribbean Court of Justice as a vital regional judicial institution and in the commitment of its judges to the principles which underpin the administration of justice throughout the Caribbean”.

World.title: ‘Dream Supreme’
World.content:
Wards of the state listen during a session at the Child Protection and Family Services Agency Transitional Living Programme Higher Education Day for Youth in State Care and Expo, held inside the Douglas Orane Auditorium, Wolmer’s Boys’, School on Thursday. Photo: JIS

TWENTY-FIVE adolescents leaving State care will receive full scholarships for tertiary education, from Supreme Ventures Foundation under its latest investment in the Child Protection and Family Services Agency (CPFSA) Transitional Living Programme (TLP).

The announcement was made by Chloleen Daley-Muschett, assistant vice-president of public relations and corporate affairs at Supreme Ventures Limited, as she delivered greetings to the TLP Higher Education Day Expo held at Wolmer’s Boys’ School on Thursday.

According to Daley-Muschett, when the foundation first partnered with CPFSA’s TLP in 2021, it awarded 20 youths with full-ride scholarships while it was celebrating its 20th anniversary.

Now that the organisation is celebrating 25 years, Daley-Muschett argued that it was only fitting to award 25 excellent and deserving adolescents with full scholarships to fulfil their academic dreams.

“When we say full [scholarship], we mean full. So tuition, accommodation, expenses, housing, everything, miscellaneous, we provided for them,” she said.

“To date, I can tell you that the foundation has invested more than $100 million. That’s $100 million into the students who have gone through the programme so far. So you can do the math; if it was $100 million for 20, you can do the math to know how much we’ll be investing for the 25 students,” said Daley-Muschett.

That investment, she said, will cover whichever path a recipient chooses, noting that even a traditionally more pricey degree, like medicine, is supported.

“So when I say dream supreme, I mean dream supreme. Don’t limit yourself… If it is something that you’re interested in and you have an aptitude to do, go out there, get the information, make yourself visible, and you never know what can happen for you, because the success of our investment depends on you,” she said.

Daley-Muschett encouraged youth at the TLP Expo to be bold and pointed out that hard work and dedication are the values that will allow them to achieve their goals.

“It depends on your drive, your focus, your own ambition. Those are the qualities that will turn the opportunity that we give to you into achievement for life for you. So to all of you today who are a part of the TLP, this day is for you. The CPFSA has gone all out to have all of these executives here for you. Use the opportunities to ask questions, explore your options, and imagine your future. Don’t limit that imagination. Dream supreme,” she reiterated.

Described as an exit-readiness project, the TLP was implemented through the collaborative efforts of the CPFSA, The University of the West Indies Open Campus, the Caribbean Child Development Centre, and the United States Agency for International Development, which provided the funding for the initial implementation.

The aim of the project is to facilitate a smooth transition to independent living for adolescents who have reached 18 years and are leaving State care.

Under the programme, the TLP youngsters are exposed to different pathways to aid in their readiness for independent living. These include life skills, coaching, entrepreneurship, vocational and technical skills training, house accommodation for two years, as well as tertiary enrolment.
