World.title: Experts: As Inflation Falls, Kazakhstan Faces New Monetary Policy Trade-Off
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s annual inflation slowed to 10.2% in July, extending its decline for a tenth consecutive month, while lending is increasingly shifting from consumer borrowing toward business financing, according to National Bank (NBK) Governor Timur Suleimenov’s report to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Aug. 13.

The figures point to a changing balance in Kazakhstan’s economy. Inflation is moving lower, and the NBK has already begun cautiously easing monetary policy, cutting the base rate to 16.75% in July. At the same time, stronger investment activity and continued quasi-fiscal stimulus are supporting faster economic growth, creating a potential limit on how quickly borrowing costs can decline further.

The National Bank’s next policy decision is scheduled for Sept. 4, when markets will be watching to see whether the regulator finds sufficient evidence that the slowdown in inflation is sustainable.

Inflation slows, creating room for cautious easing

According to Suleimenov, annual inflation declined to 10.2% in July. The slowdown follows a series of policy decisions that have gradually reduced the National Bank’s base rate. The regulator kept the rate at 18% in April, lowered it to 17% in June and then reduced it by another 25 basis points to 16.75% on July 24.

The latest reduction was significant because it marked a shift from maintaining restrictive conditions toward a cautious normalization of monetary policy. However, the National Bank has stressed that the decline in inflation does not mean the inflation problem has been resolved. In its July decision, the regulator noted that some underlying components of price growth remained elevated and inflation expectations continued to pose risks. The NBK therefore said that further decisions would depend on evidence that disinflation is sustainable, rather than on a predetermined path of rate cuts.

The central bank expects inflation to remain between 9% and 11% in 2026, then slow to 5.5%-7.5% in 2027 and approach its 5% target in 2028.

The key contradiction: growth is helping the economy but complicating inflation policy

One of the most important factors shaping the National Bank’s next steps is the strength of economic activity. According to the report, GDP growth reached 3% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026, supported by stronger-than-expected investment activity.

Investment demand is expected to remain a major driver of growth, including through quasi-fiscal financing, subsidized loans, development institutions and guarantees supporting large projects. This creates a more complicated environment for monetary policy.

Normally, lower inflation would provide a stronger argument for cutting interest rates. But faster economic growth and continued investment stimulus can increase demand and liquidity, potentially adding new pressure to prices.

The National Bank has repeatedly identified the scale and parameters of quasi-fiscal stimulus as one of the major risks to the inflation outlook. In its monetary policy assessment, it warned that active quasi-fiscal financing can partly offset the effects of tighter monetary conditions and weaken the transmission of the base rate through the economy.

In other words, Kazakhstan is entering a phase in which monetary and quasi-fiscal policies will need to be more closely coordinated. The faster the government and quasi-public sector stimulate investment and demand, the more cautious the National Bank may need to be about reducing interest rates.

Credit growth shifts toward business

Suleimenov also reported a notable change in the structure of bank lending. As of July 1, business lending had increased 17.1% year-on-year, while lending to small and medium-sized enterprises accelerated to 29.6%. Meanwhile, consumer lending growth slowed from 21% at the beginning of the year to 13%, reflecting prudential measures and a gradual normalization of retail credit growth.

The shift is important for the broader economic strategy. Kazakhstan has long faced concerns about rapid growth in household borrowing and its potential contribution to consumption-driven demand. A slowdown in consumer lending combined with faster business financing could help redirect credit toward investment and production. Earlier National Bank data showed that SMEs were already the primary source of growth in corporate lending, while mortgage lending continued to expand, supported by preferential housing programs.

Whether this shift becomes sustainable will matter. Business lending can support productivity and supply capacity over the longer term, potentially reducing inflationary pressures if financing results in higher output. But in the short term, large-scale investment spending can also increase demand for imports, labor and construction materials.

A stronger tenge offers additional support

The strengthening of the tenge has also become an important part of the recent disinflation story. According to economist Ruslan Sultanov’s analysis of July currency market data, the rate on the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange fell from 480.72 to 473.59 tenge per dollar during the month, while the weighted average rate on the over-the-counter market strengthened from approximately 486.2 to 471.4 tenge per dollar.

According to Sultanov, the strengthening occurred despite continued substantial demand for foreign currency. The Unified Accumulative Pension Fund purchased $375 million on the market in July, while the mandatory sale of part of quasi-public-sector foreign-currency revenues was suspended as of July 15.

At the same time, the National Bank did not conduct foreign exchange interventions, while sales from the National Fund totaled $200 million, and quasi-public-sector entities sold around $195 million.

“This is an interesting signal: even with significant counter‑demand from the fund and a reduction in one of the sources of the mandatory currency supply, the market still ended the month with a stronger tenge,” Sultanov wrote in his Telegram channel.

A stronger tenge can help slow inflation by reducing the cost of imported goods and limiting the pass-through of exchange-rate movements into consumer prices. The National Bank has identified the stronger currency as one of the factors supporting disinflation.

Markets expect another cut, but not a rapid easing cycle

Professional market participants surveyed by the Association of Financiers of Kazakhstan in August have become more optimistic about both inflation and the tenge. Their 12-month inflation forecast declined to 10.1%, while 60% of respondents expected the National Bank to lower the base rate to 16.5% at its Sept. 4 meeting. Another 28% expected the rate to remain unchanged at 16.75%, while 12% allowed for a rate increase.

Over a 12-month horizon, respondents expect the base rate to fall to 14.75%. Yet even this forecast points to gradual rather than aggressive easing. According to the AFK’s analytical center, the projected real interest rate would remain positive at around 4.65%, reflecting expectations that inflation risks will continue to constrain the speed of rate cuts.

That cautious outlook broadly corresponds with the National Bank’s position. The regulator has emphasized that the return to its 5% inflation target depends not only on interest rate policy, but also on fiscal consolidation, a narrowing of quasi-fiscal stimulus, stable inflation expectations and predictable tariff policies.

The Sept. 4 rate decision will therefore be about more than whether the base rate is reduced by another 25 basis points. It will provide a clearer indication of how the regulator views this trade-off: whether the recent decline in inflation is sufficient to justify a broader easing cycle, or whether Kazakhstan’s accelerating investment-driven economy will require monetary policy to remain restrictive for longer.

World.title: “When the state serves an oligarch, people leave” – from a march in Tbilisi. “Protests in Georgia” video blog
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Judges vs ordinary pensioners in Azerbaijan: what the law and figures show
World.content:
Judges and pensions in Azerbaijan

The pension of Azerbaijani judge Jahangir Yusifov was increased from 4,700 manat (around $2,765) to 7,500 manat (around $4,412) after he took the matter to court. Thanks to special pension rules, judges’ pensions can be dozens of times higher than the country’s average pension.

For comparison: the minimum labour pension in Azerbaijan is 320 manat (around $188).

When Baku Court of Appeal judge Jahangir Yusifov retired in 2025 at the age of 65, the State Social Protection Fund awarded him a monthly pension of 4,700 manat. That amount was equivalent to around 58% of his average monthly salary while serving as a judge.

Yusifov demanded that his pension be increased to 8,200 manat (around $4,824), arguing that he had worked all his life under difficult conditions, possessed special professional qualifications, and had been subject to a high level of responsibility.

The Baku Administrative Court upheld most of his claim, increasing his pension to around 7,500 manat. His request for additional financial assistance equal to 10% of his pension was rejected.

This is not the first such case. Other retired judges have filed similar claims, including Azad Majidov, Anvar Seyidov, Ulvi Mayilov and others. The courts have upheld all of the claims filed.

These cases clearly demonstrate how the special social protection mechanism provided for judges under Azerbaijani law is applied in practice.

Judges’ pension provisions

Under Article 109 of the Law “On Courts and Judges,” judges’ pensions are calculated according to special rules and depend on their length of service as a judge.

For those who have served as a judge for at least five years, the pension may be set at 45% of their average salary.

For between 5 and 10 years of service, an additional 2% is added to the 45% for each additional year.

For between 10 and 15 years of service, the pension is set at 55% of the average salary, plus 5% for each additional year, but cannot exceed 80% of the average salary.

Pension calculations also take into account pension capital and other allowances предусмотренные by law.

These higher percentage rates and additional benefits based on length of service provide judges with special pension conditions compared with other groups of the population.

Is it possible to live on a pension?

A judge’s pension of 7,500 manat (around $4,412) is 23 times higher than the minimum pension and 12–13 times higher than the average pension.

For comparison, the official subsistence minimum for a pensioner, regardless of profession, is 245 manat (around $145).

The average pension is significantly higher than this threshold. Nevertheless, it can be difficult for a single pensioner to maintain a stable standard of living solely on an average pension. Older people often need additional sources of income, such as employment, family support or targeted social assistance.

According to official statistics, as of April 1, 2026, more than 105,000 old-age pension recipients were still working.

But state officials, prosecutors and judges are provided with a fundamentally different level of social protection. Many people in Azerbaijan view this approach as a “double standard” enshrined in law. And when it comes to lawsuits filed by judges seeking higher pensions, public discussions often include comments along the lines of: “Apparently, even that wasn’t enough for the judges.”

News in Azerbaijan

World.title: Heavy rain floods streets, basements and metro stations in Tbilisi – video
World.content:
Heavy rain in Tbilisi

Following heavy rainfall overnight on 14 August, the Georgian capital was once again flooded. Tbilisi City Hall issued a statement on the situation, saying the intense rainfall had “caused certain problems”.

According to the city authorities, central districts were the worst affected. Private homes and basements were flooded, while a retaining wall at one residential property collapsed. Streets across the city and areas around several metro stations were also inundated.

Throughout the night, residents posted videos from different parts of the capital showing flooded streets and squares. Residents of one street in the city centre also blocked the road, calling for help in dealing with the damage.

Videos published by city residents:

“The heavy rainfall in the capital caused problems in all ten districts. Gravel and stones were washed onto roads. Our staff are carrying out clean-up work around the clock. The rain was particularly heavy in the Vake, Mtatsminda and Krtsanisi districts.

“More than 500 personnel and 30 pieces of equipment have been mobilised across all affected areas and are involved in the clean-up operation. The work will continue until all the problems have been fully resolved,” said Giorgi Papava, head of Tbilisi’s main municipal services operator, Tbilservice Group.

World.title: More than 32,000 applications for Armenian citizenship in a year: who is applying and why
World.content:
Rise in applications for Armenian citizenship

“There has been a sharp increase in the number of applications for Armenian citizenship. In 2025, the number exceeded 32,000, a historic high for the entire history of the Republic of Armenia,” said Armen Kazaryan, acting deputy interior minister.

According to him, the number of citizenship applications exceeded 20,000 in each of the previous two years, compared with 7,000-8,000 in earlier years.

Kazaryan believes the main goal of applicants is to obtain a document that allows them to travel:

“We have seen certain developments, in particular the outbreak of hostilities in Ukraine and restrictions on travel for Russian citizens. After that, we saw an increase in applications for Armenian citizenship. By the way, most Russian citizens applying for Armenian citizenship are ethnic Armenians.”

He rejected claims that obtaining Armenian citizenship is a complicated process:

“The requirements for ethnic Armenians are ‘zero’. People may face administrative difficulties. For example, some may lack the necessary documents proving their ethnicity, or their records may contain errors. In such cases, we need to compare the information with other records and verify it. Essentially, Armenia imposes no requirements on ethnic Armenians.”

Kazaryan himself considers the lack of requirements for ethnic Armenians problematic. In his view, this devalues the institution of citizenship itself.

“We will soon present a draft of the relevant legislative amendments addressing these issues,” he said, without specifying what changes the amendments would introduce.

Border crossings: more people entered than left

Nelli Davtyan, acting head of the Migration and Citizenship Service, also spoke to journalists. She recalled that last year Armenia recorded a “significant positive figure” in the difference between the number of citizens entering and leaving the country. The figure stood at 8,660.

In the first half of this year, the difference between entries and exits stood at 1,347.

“There were 871,409 entries and 870,062 exits. If we compare this with figures for the first half of previous years, last year’s figure was -20,065, while in 2024 it was -22,893,” Davtyan noted.

She stressed that the figure usually rises in the second half of the year. This happens because seasonal migrant workers return home after leaving the country for temporary work. They usually leave in early spring and return in autumn. Davtyan therefore described a positive figure already in the first half of the year as “exceptional”.

More than 6,000 people granted temporary residence permits

Armen Kazaryan said Armenia had transformed from a country that “sends” migrants abroad into a country that receives migrants. “The second major trend is the growing interest in Armenia among foreign nationals,” he noted.

Nelli Davtyan said the Migration and Citizenship Service had received 9,534 applications for one-year temporary residence permits: “Of these, 6,059 were approved. Compared with previous years, the number of applications has almost tripled. The proportion of approved applications has also nearly tripled.”

According to Davtyan, the number of applications for three-year residence permits has also increased, although more modestly: “In previous years, the figure stood at 1,500-1,700, while in the first half of this year it had already reached 2,085.”

Armenia implementing 53 EU recommendations on visa liberalisation

Armen Kazaryan said Armenia was actively cooperating with the European Union on visa liberalisation. He recalled that Armenia received its first report on the implementation of the action plan in May 2026. The report gave a fairly positive assessment of the steps taken by the Armenian government.

“The EU presented us with 53 recommendations. To complete our work, we divided them into specific actions. We broke down the recommendations so that we could clearly identify the steps we need to take to implement them,” Kazaryan explained.

Based on the 53 recommendations, an Armenian working group drew up a list of 117 actions. More than half of them have already been completed.

The recommendations form part of the first stage of the visa liberalisation action plan. This stage covers legislation and policy development only. The authorities expect to assess how effectively Armenia has implemented the first stage by early 2027 or during the first half of the year. If the results prove positive, work on the second stage will begin.

Rise in applications for Armenian citizenship

World.title: Myth Detector: 230 fake social media accounts created to create illusion of support for Georgian PM’s statements
World.content:
Fake accounts created to support Georgia’s prime minister

1On 2 August, marking the 18th anniversary of the 2008 August War, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze held a briefing. He focused in particular on what he described as the spread of “Russophobia” in Georgia and the role of the so-called “deep state” in this process.

After the briefing, pro-government messages began circulating widely on social media. Various media outlets also published visual materials promoting these messages.

According to a study by Myth Detector, 230 fake accounts took part in the campaign. The organisation analysed likes on social media posts, as well as the photos and activity of the profiles that shared them. It identified signs of coordinated and suspicious behaviour that, according to the study, aimed to increase support for specific government narratives.

The study also says the profiles were designed to appear as if they belonged to different socio-demographic groups. Some accounts used photographs depicting idyllic family life to make themselves appear more trustworthy.

Profile photos were generated using artificial intelligence (AI)

According to Hive Moderation, a tool for detecting AI-generated images, there was more than a 90% probability that all 230 profile photos had been generated using AI. In some cases, the probability reached 100%. A visual inspection also identified features typical of AI-generated images, including unnatural shapes of hands and fingers, as well as certain distortions.

The photos repeat the same settings and compositions

Some accounts use identical or very similar photos, including the same images with minor changes. The visual design of different accounts also repeats similar photography styles and details. These include photos with a consistent aesthetic, featuring Tbilisi in the background, a glass of wine or a cup of coffee, a hand touching the head, or similar compositional choices. The accounts also use images showing people having fun, relaxing or taking part in sports to create an impression of authenticity. In some cases, different accounts use the same first and last names.

An illusion of broad support is created through artificially diverse social and demographic profiles

The campaign creates the impression that it brings together people of different ages, appearances and interests. The profiles include young and older people, supporters of conservative and alternative views, as well as religious people, family-oriented users, sports enthusiasts and people who enjoy outdoor activities.

AI-generated accounts use real workplaces and educational institutions to make their profiles appear more credible

Most profiles list places of education and employment, including the Tbilisi Transport Company, various Georgian insurance companies, commercial banks, microfinance organisations, government agencies and municipal services.

Different accounts show identical behaviour

Most profiles list a date between 20 and 24 July 2026 as the date they began living in Georgian cities, although some accounts appear to have been created earlier.

Profile activity focuses on the same messages

The activity of the suspicious accounts, particularly their likes, is concentrated on posts featuring conspiracy claims by the ruling party’s chairman about the “party of global war”, the “deep state’s plan” and the “opening of a second front”. They also engage with the narrative about “Russophobia”, suggesting an artificial increase in the level of support.

Fake accounts created to support Georgia’s prime minister

World.title: Russia no longer attracts Armenian migrant workers as they look for new opportunities in Europe
World.content:
Armenian workers turn to Europe instead of Russia

The geography of labour migration from Armenia is changing. Russia, which until recently remained the main destination, has become less attractive. The main reasons are Russia’s economic downturn, driven by the war in Ukraine, and the depreciation of the rouble.

Many migrants are now returning from Russia to Armenia. Some are trying to find work in their home villages or in the capital, while others are looking for new opportunities, particularly in Europe. The direction of labour migration is changing, with European countries becoming increasingly popular.

Work visa for Poland

After two years working at a meat-processing plant in Poland, 40-year-old Serob (name changed) returned to Armenia for a month. He came to prepare all the necessary documents and take his wife and children with him to Warsaw.

“I received a three-year residence permit and the right to work. Living away from my family is difficult. I decided that we should be together. I should also say that Poland has become one of the first steps towards the European labour market for many people. Many of my friends work in the Czech Republic, the Netherlands and other countries on legal work visas. I was also offered a job in the Netherlands, but I decided to stay in Poland,” he says.

Serob is a butcher. He was also in demand in Armenia. However, he says his salary there was not enough to support his family:

“I had friends who worked as butchers in Europe. They told me that the profession was in demand there and well paid. Gradually, I started thinking: why not try going to Europe and working there? I also had a lot of debts and loans. I went to Poland on a work visa. The process moved slowly. The Polish embassy invited me for an interview a year after I submitted my application.”

A recruitment agency then sent his details to a meat-processing company. Representatives of the company interviewed Serob online. During the video call, he demonstrated his professional skills to the employer, including how he deboned meat.

“The employer liked my work and sent me a contract and the necessary documents. The embassy then approved my work visa. At first, I lived in a house in Poland with people of different nationalities. They all worked for the same company and lived in separate rooms. Later, when my financial situation improved, I moved into a separate flat with a friend from Armenia. I sent most of my earnings to my family to help resolve our financial problems. I did not work in a shop or at a market. I worked at a specialised meat-processing plant with refrigerated storage facilities. It is physically demanding work,” the butcher says.

He notes a shortage of butchers in the European labour market, which creates demand for migrants with the necessary skills. Meat-processing plants employ workers from Ukraine, Argentina, Azerbaijan and Armenia.

“Many Armenians are now going to European countries for work. And not only to meat-processing plants. When I flew to Poland, I met some women who worked as pastry chefs on the plane. They were also travelling to Poland under legal employment contracts. Many Armenians also work in shops. These are people who speak foreign languages. In any case, I am happy. I will return to work in a month, this time with my family,” Serob says.

Working at a German medical clinic with an Armenian degree

Doctors, teachers and highly skilled professionals in various fields are also in demand on the European labour market. Dentist Edgar Mirzoyan has been living and working in Germany for nine months.

Edgar Mirzoyan

“One day, my nurse told me that her friend worked in Germany and that they might need a dentist. I simply gave her my contact details and forgot about it. Some time later, they contacted me. At the same time, I started learning German. The whole process took two years: learning the language, preparing documents and taking exams. Finally, I moved to Germany. By the way, getting my Armenian degree recognised in Germany seemed more realistic and achievable than in other European countries,” Edgar says.

At the same time, the 30-year-old dentist studied not only the professional requirements but also the overall situation in the country, including its economy, level of safety and even happiness index.

“Geography also influenced my final decision. It was important for me to stay connected to Armenia. You can get from Germany to Armenia in just a few hours. In this sense, Europe was a much more convenient destination for me than, for example, Canada. Before moving to Germany, I had a completely different idea of what it would be like. Of course, everyone’s experience is different. Some doctors who arrived at the same time as me had a much harder journey. A lot depends on which city you move to, who your employer is and who you interact with. Everyone has their own experience,” he says.

Edgar started working two days after arriving in Germany. Some time later, his wife also joined him.

“Before moving to Germany, I registered in advance to take a language exam. They tested my knowledge of medical German. I passed the exam successfully. After that, I received a temporary licence valid for two years. I can work during this period, but I must work under the supervision of an experienced doctor.

However, the process of having my degree fully recognised is still under way. The authorities compare my entire university curriculum, the number of hours I completed and the subjects I studied with the German curriculum. I applied for this process while I was still in Armenia. They only started reviewing my documents after two years of waiting. If they find differences between the curricula, I will have to make up the gaps. It is not yet clear how significant those differences will be,” the doctor says.

According to Edgar, working in Germany has its own particularities. Berlin is a multicultural city, and his patients include not only Germans. About 30 per cent are Armenians and Yazidis, while another 30 per cent are Russians and Ukrainians.

Edgar continues to practise in Armenia as well:

“I can take leave twice a year. I come to Armenia, mainly perform implant procedures and surgeries, and then return to Germany. I have many patients who wait for me to come back. They book appointments in advance, I come and perform the surgery, and the next stage of treatment takes place three to six months later, when I can return again.”

When labour migration is a family choice

For many people who move to Europe, leaving is a decision about their family’s future, improving their living conditions and trying to build a new life in a different environment.

Vergine (name changed) chose this path. She has lived in the Czech Republic with her husband for seven years and now has two children.

“First, my husband moved to Prague on a work visa. He started working in the security department of a shopping centre. Two years later, I joined him. We made the decision consciously, after carefully considering everything. We wanted to settle down and continue our lives in a European country. In this sense, the Czech Republic seemed like a suitable option, and we are very happy with our choice,” Vergine says.

Before moving to the Czech Republic, the couple worked at Zvartnots Airport.

“At first, I worked at a language centre as an English teacher. Then my second child was born here. Of course, there were many difficulties. We lived in a foreign country without support from relatives and with a small child, but we managed. I now work as an English teacher at a school,” she says.

The young family does not plan to return to Armenia for now, but they regularly visit their relatives.

“We have the right to live and work here, but I am sure that one day we will definitely return,” Vergine says.

Changing migration patterns

According to Tatevik Bezhanian, an expert with the migration programme of the charitable organisation Armenian Caritas, Armenia currently has no statistics showing how many people leave for European countries to work.

One reason is that Armenia has no intergovernmental labour migration agreements with EU countries. Bulgaria is the only exception. In addition, most people who leave for Europe find jobs through private recruitment agencies, and the state does not register this process.

“You will not find this data in official statistics. On the other hand, we also do not have a migration card system under which people have to state when entering or leaving the country that they are going abroad to work. They may not indicate the purpose of their departure at all,” Bezhanian says.

She says this problem is not unique to Armenia. Internationally, governments mainly register migrant workers arriving in their countries because they can manage these migration flows. Countries that pursue targeted labour migration policies, sign bilateral agreements and organise the recruitment of their citizens abroad usually have comprehensive data on those who leave. The Philippines and Uzbekistan are among them, for example.

Tatevik Bezhanian notes that even when Armenian authorities want information about labour migrants leaving for Russia, they have to rely on official Russian statistics:

“If the geography of labour migration expands, we will have to approach the relevant authorities in countries such as Poland, the Czech Republic and the Netherlands. We will need to obtain data and determine how many Armenian citizens work there.”

Armenian workers turn to Europe instead of Russia

World.title: Opinion on Georgian petrol in Abkhazia: ‘If needed, it’s possible’
World.content:
The indirect consequence of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries has been a fuel crisis in Abkhazia, which in recent years has been buying petrol from Russia.

After struggling with shortages for two weeks, Abkhazia decided to buy petrol from Georgia. Given the unresolved Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, this was a rather “unorthodox” move, but at the same time the only viable way out of the situation.

In a blog post, Inal Khashig, editor of the Abkhaz outlet Chegemskaya Pravda, discusses whether Abkhazia can trade with Georgia.

Inal Khashig: “Abkhazia has been grappling with a petrol shortage for the past two weeks. There is virtually no fuel left in the country. Government assurances that the situation is under control and that a new shipment of petrol is about to arrive have done little to reassure people — if anything, they have only deepened the pessimism. Queues at petrol stations stretch as far as the eye can see.

And then petrol arrived from an unexpected source — Georgia.

Tbilisi says the government has nothing to do with it and that it is entirely a private business matter. Sukhumi, for its part, says that when the country is facing a fuel shortage, it will not prevent petrol tankers from entering from Georgia. After all, there is precedent for this kind of economic contact: during the difficult 1990s, we supplied Georgians with relatively cheap fuel.

This particular fuel crisis has once again brought an enduring Abkhaz question to the fore: should we trade with an enemy state or not?”

To me, it is quite straightforward: if this kind of cooperation is vital for the country as a whole, its economy and the well-being of its people, then it is justified. Sukhumi has, after all, cooperated with Tbilisi in the energy sector throughout the post-war years, and no one objects because there is no alternative. This cooperation is vital to both Abkhazia and Georgia.

And now, when the whole of Abkhazia — and with it the country’s economy — has ground to a halt because of the lack of petrol, refusing to buy fuel from the Georgians looks like outright posturing.

Incidentally, I think the government’s argument that Abkhazia actively sold petrol to Georgia in the 1990s is a very good one. At the time, war-ravaged Abkhazia was under a severe blockade: Russia under Boris Yeltsin had effectively sealed us off on all sides. Nothing could be brought in or taken out. About the only thing permitted was taking mandarins across the border in handcarts, with Abkhaz women effectively serving as beasts of burden.

Abkhazia’s tiny budget was funded by selling timber and scrap metal to Turkey, as well as by smuggling fuel into Georgia.

The latter involved considerable risk and loss of life, as fuel tankers had to travel towards the Georgian border through the Gali district, which was unstable at the time. But there was effectively no other way of bringing even a little money into the state coffers. Whatever anyone may say, those modest revenues helped Abkhazia survive at the time.

And yes, we traded with Georgia then because we had to.

And we need to do so now to protect the country from a fuel crisis.

And in future, we need to take similarly responsible steps, even if they run counter to established dogmas. Rigid dogma is not the best guide to action in crises like the one we are facing now.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Analysts say Ukraine is preparing a large-scale offensive
World.content:
Ukraine Launches Large-Scale Offensive

Based on reporting by Novosti Donbassa

Ukrainian defense forces have liberated 19 settlements across several sectors of the front, according to DeepState, a Ukrainian battlefield monitoring project, which reported the advances after updating its combat map.

According to the analysts, Ukrainian forces have regained control of Zelenyi Hai, Novokhatske, Hrushevske, Tolstoi, Zirka, Yalta, Piddubne, Myrne, Voskresenka, Sichneve, Vorone, Ternove, Berezove, Stepne, Kalynovske, Pryvillia, Zlahoda, Rybne and Krasnohorske.

In addition, Ukrainian troops pushed Russian forces back in six other settlements: Novopavlivka, Novoheorhiivka, Novomykolaivka, Novohryhorivka, Zaporizke and Pryvilne.

The Ukrainian military also released video footage from settlements it said had been liberated in the Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions.

World.title: Study warns of measles risk with 1.7 million Australians vulnerable
World.content:
An estimated 1.7 million Australians are not protected against measles, putting the country at risk of more outbreaks, according to new analysis from the peak immunisation research organisation.

The National Centre for Immunisation Research and Surveillance (NCIRS) study found almost seven per cent of the population was susceptible to measles in 2019.

The paper will be published today in the Australian and New Zealand Journal of Public Health, and lead author Zoë Croker said susceptibility was high for key age groups of Australians born from the late 1970s onwards.

80,000 kids aged five and under behind on vaccinations The latest immunisation data shows more than 80,000 Australian children aged five and under are not fully up to date with their vaccinations.

The number of people susceptible included Australian babies who were not yet eligible for measles immunisations.

"The concern is that there will be more measles outbreaks that will be harder to contain," Ms Crocker said.

"We'll start to see more cases and a higher chance of there being a death associated."

'A warning sign'

Ms Crocker said the world-first study combined blood samples testing measles immunity, with vaccination data and represents the most comprehensive national estimate currently possible.

The analysis found overall measles immunity was 93.3 per cent, which epidemiologist Adrian Esterman said Australians must take as a "warning sign".

"[That] is not good enough. That means that we are at risk of getting major measles outbreaks," Professor Esterman said.

"We don't really want it to get any worse."

The number of people susceptible includes Australian babies not yet eligible for measles immunisations. (iStockPhoto/saritwuttisan)

The World Health Organization has a target of achieving 93-95 per cent vaccine coverage, to establish herd immunity and prevent the spread of measles.

Australia achieved measles elimination status in 2014 but continues to have imported cases in overseas visitors and returning residents.

There were very few measles cases in Australia during the pandemic, but numbers have increased in the past two years.

Who is at risk and why should we be worried?

Anyone who is not fully vaccinated is at risk. Babies and young children are particularly at risk because they are not routinely vaccinated until 12 months old. So are those with reduced immunity and unvaccinated pregnant women because they can not be immunised while pregnant.

The paper identified the key age groups with higher levels of susceptibility to measles, which included infants and young children and people aged 42-49 years, 31-33 years and 25 and 26 years.

Ms Crocker said those groups were highly susceptible because of generational gaps in immunisation programs.

Zoë Crocker says we could start to see more cases and a higher chance of death. (Supplied)

"The biggest gaps are in people born around the year 2000, as well as those born in 1993, 1994 and 1995, which was when that second dose of measles-containing vaccine was introduced," she said.

"Close behind are people in the early vaccine era, so born in 1977 to 1983… they're more likely to only have a single dose of measles-containing vaccine."

Ms Croker said people born during or since 1966 may also be more susceptible because they may have missed vaccination altogether or only be partially vaccinated.

However, she said some of these people may have life-long immunity from childhood measles infections.

Professor Esterman, from Adelaide University, said the numbers were daunting.

"We are at that stage where we need to be worried, we do not want our coverage rates to drop any more than they are now," he said.

"If a single infectious person goes into a room with a group of people who haven't got immunity, they will infect, very quickly, 12 to 15 of them. It's the most infectious disease we know about."

What is measles? Measles is a very contagious viral illness

Symptoms include fever, cough, red eyes and a red or blotchy rash

Measles can lead to serious complications including ear infections, pneumonia and encephalitis (inflammation of the brain)

Vaccination is the best way to prevent measles

Overseas travellers urged to get another jab

Travellers are a higher risk of bringing measles into Australia, according to NCIRS associate director Frank Beard.

"We'd strongly encourage people in the current climate of increasing global outbreaks of measles to check … records of measles vaccination," Dr Beard said.

"If they haven't had good evidence that they previously received two doses at any time, then we strongly encourage them to get vaccinated again."

The World Health Organization has a target of achieving 93-95 per cent vaccine coverage. (Reuters: Jayla Whitfield-Anderson)

Professor Esterman said those aged between 20 and 40 years old were catching measles during overseas travel.

"Almost all of those cases are coming from people who've gone to Asia, so it could be the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand, where they have quite large measles outbreaks … they come back and bring it with them," he said.

"There's a huge role here for GPs. If a patient is going overseas and talks to a GP about what they need in terms of protection, the GP should immediately ask them, what's your measles status like?"

Dr Beard said he would "strongly encourage" all adults in the at-risk age groups to consider getting another measles vaccine.

'We'll see more outbreaks'

Ms Crocker said measles would circulate more throughout Australia if herd immunity dipped below 93 per cent.

"It means that our public health system is less likely to be able to chase down every case and we are at a greater risk of measles then becoming more prominent in Australia."

The dark side of addressing vaccine hesitancy in Australia Addressing vaccine hesitancy requires skill and patience – some days, the people who do it feel like they’re drowning in a sea of lies.

Professor Esterman fears Australia will fall below the threshold for herd immunity, which will lead to "more and more outbreaks".

"It does mean that there will be some pockets of the Australian population which have got much lower coverage than that and that's where you start seeing these small outbreaks occurring," he said.

"It's in those pockets of the population, which have got lower coverage rates.

"This is telling us that there's something wrong, which we need to do something about."

The latest immunisation data shows childhood vaccination coverage declined for a fifth year in 2025.

Ms Crocker said her paper may "underestimate" susceptibility to measles, given childhood immunisation rates have dropped in recent years.

World.title: Four paintings by Renaissance artist stolen from Italian museum
World.content:
Four artworks by 15th century painter Antonello da Messina have been stolen overnight from the Museo Regionale di Messina according to Italy's culture minister.

Culture minister Alessandro Giuli spoke on Sunday, expressing confidence in the police inquiry.

The stolen art is parts of the only surviving work by the Renaissance painter to have remained in his native city, as well as a small painting acquired by the Sicilian Region two decades ago.

"Christ in Pieta", the reverse side of a double-sided devotional panel stolen in the heist. (Museo Regionale Accascina Messina via Reuters)

"I've learnt of the theft with shock and sadness," Mr Giuli said in a statement.

Italian media reported the thieves entered the museum on the night of August 15, a national holiday in Italy.

A museum official contacted by Reuters said they could not provide any information.

Sale for $15 million put museum on radar

Enzo Caruso, a local councillor in charge of culture, told Italian media outlet Corriere della Sera that the heist "was almost out of a movie".

Mr Caruso said the purchase of one Messina artwork by the Italian state for $US15 million ($21 million) earlier this year may have put the museum on the criminals' radar.

Local council believes the recent sale of a Messina painting for $US 15 million made the museum a target. (AP Photo: Gregorio Borgia)

The thieves took three of five remaining panels that made up an altarpiece known as Polittico di San Gregorio.

Originally comprising six panels and destined for a local monastery that was destroyed by the 1908 earthquake in Messina, the altarpiece was the only work by the Sicilian painter never to have left his hometown.

The thieves took a fourth artwork from a secure display case, a small two-sided painting depicting the Virgin with Child and a Franciscan monk on one side and Christ on the other.

The work was part of the Wilhelm Soldan collection and was sold by global auction house, Christie's, to the Sicilian Region in 2003, the year it was attributed to Antonello da Messina.

Multiple art thefts

Fine art recovered after three-minute Italian museum heist Three century-old paintings stolen by an organised gang from an Italian museum have been recovered.

In February, Italy's culture ministry bought another two-sided painting, known as Ecce Homo, from Sotheby's just before it was to be sold at auction.

The Messina theft took place after Italian police on Friday recovered three paintings by French masters Paul Cezanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse.

The three paintings were stolen from a museum near the northern city of Parma in March.

Reuters

World.title: Gangland boss Fadi Haddara shot in Melbourne's inner west
World.content:
Alleged gangland boss Fadi Haddara has been shot in Melbourne's inner west.

Multiple police and underworld sources have told the ABC that Haddara was ambushed outside his Altona North home on Marigold Avenue late this evening.

Haddara's condition remains unclear.

Victoria Police and Ambulance Victoria have been contacted for comment.

Haddara is allegedly the head of his namesake family crime clan, who have been long-term rivals of jailed tobacco kingpin Kazem Hamad and his 313 gang, also known as The Commission.

The Haddara clan has long been suspected of being involved in Victoria's illicit tobacco trade.

Police investigating the tobacco wars last year dropped multiple gun possession and handling stolen goods charges against Fadi Haddara.

Haddara, 48, was born in Lebanon and arrived in Australia when he was six.

He dropped out of school in year 11 and worked in security before becoming a figure in Australian kickboxing, becoming both a fighter and promoter.

In 2009 his brother, Mohammed Haddara, was killed in a drive-by shooting on Fifth Avenue, just hundreds of metres away from Sunday's incident.

World.title: Indonesia earthquake death toll reaches 53, thousands evacuated
World.content:
Thousands of evacuees are waiting for help on Indonesia's Flores island after Saturday's powerful earthquake killed at least 53 people, injured dozens and damaged hundreds of houses and buildings.

Authorities have since recorded 995 aftershocks, but only 46 were felt by residents, said National Disaster Management Agency's chief for disaster prevention Abdul Muhari, adding that 135 people were injured.

About 5,000 people fled their homes as the magnitude-7.7 quake hit the island, a spokesman for the agency, Berton Suar Pelita Panjaitan, said.

At least 24 people died in Manggarai regency and 17 in neighbouring East Manggarai, with additional fatalities reported in Sikka, Ngada and Ende regencies, the agency said in a statement.

Health workers tend to a patient on a stretcher outside at a regional hospital in Ruteng, Manggarai, East Nusa Tenggara province. (Reuters: Terisno Adon)

The quake destroyed more than 900 homes and damaged nearly 450 more and at least 167 public facilities, including schools, health centres and churches, were also damaged, the agency said.

The epicentre of the shallow quake was located just off the north coast of the island, geological authorities said.

The quake also struck Labuan Bajo, the gateway to Komodo National Park, one of Indonesia's best-known tourist destinations.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese extended his "deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who have lost their lives".

Mr Albanese said on Sunday there were no indications at this stage that Australians had been affected but authorities continued to make inquiries.

Australians in impacted areas should follow the advice of Indonesian authorities, he said.

'We need food'

Villagers spent the night after an earthquake in an open field in Nangahale village in Sikka, East Nusa Tenggara. (AFP: Arnold Weilanto)

Authorities said restoring electricity and communications as well as delivering aid to remote villages isolated by landslides remained among the biggest challenges following the quake.

"We need food, drink, medicines, and diapers for the children," Umri, a resident of Nangahale village on the north coast of Flores, told AFP on Sunday morning.

The 55-year-old, who like many Indonesians uses one name, has been hiding out on a hilltop for 24 hours with others afraid to return home.

Loading...

Nurhidayati, also 55, spent the night on a mat on the same hill.

"I'm still terrified. My heart is pounding hard remembering yesterday's tremor," she said.

"We just ran up here yesterday. I'm very scared now, still traumatised by the quake in 1992. I don't dare to go home."

People 'trapped in buildings' after earthquake Rescue teams are combing the rubble of buildings for survivors after the magnitude-7.7 earthquake struck eastern Indonesia.

Flores was struck by a magnitude-7.7 earthquake in 1992 that triggered a tsunami and killed about 2,500 people.

"I hope the government will soon distribute logistics to help us," Nurhidayati said.

"In addition to the loss of life, the offshore earthquake caused material losses that have paralysed residents' daily activities," Mr Berton said.

Mr Berton said survivors were in urgent need of assistance in the form of emergency tents, food, medicines, blankets, camp beds, mats, clean water and electricity generators.

Search continues

A view of a damaged building following an earthquake in East Nusa Tenggara province. (Reuters: Stringer)

Rescuers on Sunday dug through debris looking for people feared buried beneath landslides triggered by the quake, but there were no reports of people buried or missing.

"We have cleared most landslides and reopened roads to previously isolated villages, although communication disruptions and power outages continue to hamper search efforts," said Fathur Rahman, head of the Search and Rescue Office in Maumere, the capital of Sikka regency.

Earthquake strikes off coast of Indonesia A magnitude-7.7 earthquake strikes off the coast of Indonesia in the Flores region, killing 47, damaging buildings and triggering an early tsunami warning that has since been cancelled.

Relief workers have begun distributing rice, ready-to-eat meals, drinking water, blankets and medicine, while emergency shelters were being set up for displaced residents.

The East Nusa Tenggara provincial government that includes Flores "is processing a decree to establish an emergency response status for the next 14 days," Mr Berton said.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said on Saturday that preparations were under way to bring aid to thousands in temporary shelters.

The government sent 50,000 aid packages weighing a total of 275 tonnes to the area and European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen offered help from the bloc's Copernicus Earth observation satellites.

"Europe stands ready to deploy Copernicus, our eyes in the sky, to support search and rescue efforts. Indonesia, we stand with you," she wrote on X.

Tsunami warning lifted

After Saturday's quake, Flores residents ran for the hills as the sea retreated, a possible sign of an approaching tsunami.

Loading...

A tsunami warning was later lifted, but authorities urged people not to return to damaged buildings for fear that aftershocks may bring them down.

Waves of up to 1.6 metres were reported in some coastal regions, according to Indonesia's BMKG geological agency.

Indonesia experiences frequent earthquakes due to its location in the Pacific "Ring of Fire", an arc of intense seismic activity stretching from Japan through Southeast Asia and across the Pacific basin.

A devastating magnitude-9.1 tremor in 2004 struck off the coast of Sumatra and triggered a tsunami that killed 220,000 throughout the region, about 170,000 of them in Indonesia.

It was one of the deadliest natural disasters in recorded history.

ABC/wires

World.title: Sam Neill wins posthumous award as Sam Pang takes Gold Logie — as it happened
World.content:
Speaking in the media room after being inducted into the Logies Hall of Fame, Andrew Denton reflected on the state of satire on the ABC.

The presenter cut his teeth on shows like The Money or the Gun, where he asked provocative questions of the public, and he's not sure something like it could be made today.

"Back in the day when we made The Money or the Gun, the ABC's editorial policy was: 'You make the show, and if we don't like it, we'll let you know.' "Now I think there's more an attitude of: 'Be really careful, and if we don't like it, then we might take it off air.' "Mel Brooks put it best: 'Tragedy is when I cut my finger. Comedy is when you walk into an open sewer and die.' It's the perfect definition of comedy. It's about where you stand. "Yes, you can step over the line. Yes, offence can be caused, and you can apologise for that offence. But satire is so important in terms of holding up a bent mirror to what's going on."

In terms of making more space for young talent on our screens, offering opportunities as he spoke about in his speech, he'd like to see "a sense of courage and a sense of adventure" from TV networks including the ABC. (Which he would also like to see be better funded.)

World.title: Death in Tasmanian prison after reports man 'unresponsive' in cell
World.content:
A 23-year-old man has died while being held in custody at the Hobart Reception Centre, Tasmania Police said.

Police said prison staff alerted them to the man's death after they found him unresponsive in his cell just before 11am on Sunday.

Tasmania Police Assistant Commissioner Doug Oosterloo said the deceased man was from New Norfolk, north of Hobart.

He had been arrested on Saturday in relation to a wounding incident in Claremont the day before, and was transferred to the Hobart Reception Centre about 5:30pm, police said.

The New Norfolk man had been in custody for one night before being found unresponsive. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

"Ambulance Tasmania crews were called, Hobart uniform police attended and Hobart reception prison staff all attempted to revive the man," Assistant Commissioner Oosterloo said.

" But tragically those attempts were unsuccessful. "

Assistant Commissioner Oosterloo said forensic specialists, detectives from Tasmania Police's professional standards unit and the coroner had attended the scene.

"The professional standards investigation includes examining CCTV footage at Hobart Reception, records and interviewing all witnesses, and that is information that will come out in the investigation," he said.

Tasmania Prison Service acting director Tristan Bell said the service would not comment further, with the matter being referred to the coroner.

"On behalf of the Tasmania Prison Service, I extend my sincere condolences to the family and friends of the deceased man at this difficult time," Mr Bell said.

Claremont incident 'targeted', police say

On Friday about 5am, police responded to reports of an assault at a home on Curlew Parade, Claremont, which they believe to be a targeted incident.

Police said they were told two people had entered the residence and assaulted two occupants.

A man his 20s was shot in the hip and is now in hospital in a serious condition.

The other occupant, a woman in her 20s, was reportedly struck multiple times with the side of an axe.

She received medical treatment but was not hospitalised, police said.

Police did not confirm what role the deceased man was alleged to have played, if any, in the incident.

World.title: ‘It’s different’: Robert Irwin’s razzle-dazzle gets big thumbs up from Sam Pang
World.content:
CultureTV & radioLogies ‘It’s different’: Robert Irwin’s razzle-dazzle gets big thumbs up from Sam Pang Karl Quinn August 17, 2026 — 1:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sam Pang has won the Gold Logie for the most popular person on Australian television. And in a showstopping surprise that capped an uncommonly entertaining ceremony, he was presented with the award by a tattered and torn Sharon Strzelecki – Magda Szubanski in her first public appearance since her prolonged cancer battle – dressed in Australia Zoo fatigues and looking for all the world like she’d just emerged from a tussle with a crocodile. “I grew up watching television at the feet of my parents – they wouldn’t let me on the couch,” Pang joked in his acceptance speech. “But when you’re watching television in this country, you never think you’re going to be on it.” Sam Pang poses with his Gold Logie Award for most popular personality on Australian television during the 66th TV WEEK Logie Awards. Getty Images for TV Week Speaking in the media room backstage, he said it was a particular honour to receive the top award on a night when Deborah Mailman and Andrew Denton were being inducted into the Logie Awards Hall of Fame. “I’ve become close with [Denton] over the last few years, and then for Sharon to be there, it was all surreal,” said Pang.



In a world that sometimes feels hopelessly shrouded in gloom and conflict, the 66th TV Week Logie Awards landed as something as welcome as it was unexpected – a warm embrace that did its very best to encompass Australia in all its breadth, strangeness and diversity. And Pang’s win, which makes him the second non-white person to take home the top gong, provided its perfect end. Related Article Logies Logies 2026 as it happened: Sam Pang wins Gold Logie; touching tributes to Sam Neill and Johnny Young; Deborah Mailman inducted into Hall of Fame This is the 70th year of television in this country, and while there are those who’d happily write its obituary, Sunday night’s ceremony showed there’s life in the old dog yet, and a good deal of love for it, too. The choice of Robert Irwin as host was inspired. Groomed almost since birth to perform in the spotlight, he shouldered the unenviable task of fronting Australian TV’s favourite piñata – everyone loves to take a swing – with grace, humour, and a tight-fitting single-lapel tuxedo whose buttons seemed designed to pop open at the merest ripple of a well-honed torso. Wardrobe malfunction? Only if the fasteners didn’t pop as planned. He danced, he joked, he shed his tux for the more familiar khaki bushwear, he draped an enormous snake around the tensed neck and shoulders of the never not-tense Luke McGregor, he did the worm on stage with Peking Duk. Yes, Pang was a tough act to follow, but with his distinctive style of enviro-showbiz razzle-dazzle, Irwin made this show his own.



Loading He stamped his mark from the beginning, with a pre-recorded skit that incorporated Russell Coight, Glenn Robbin’s caricature of an Irwinesque figure. Then, as the ceremony proper kicked off, Irwin delivered a heartfelt acknowledgement to country, almost certainly the first-ever acknowledgement of that sort to grace a Logies. On a night on which Mailman basked in a standing ovation and the palpable love in the room, Goolagong won best miniseries, its star Lila McGuire was voted most popular newcomer, and so many other nominees were First Nations people, it was more than fitting. Before the bleaters at Sky, now known as News24, start crowing about cultural elites, take note that this Logies made space for everyone. After RFDS won best drama – pipping the world-class Narrow Road to the Deep North, which started the evening as the most nominated program but ended it with just one win, for Simon Baker as best supporting actor – Emma Hamilton tried to put her finger on why the show matters. Luke McGregor has an awkward encounter with a snake. Getty Images for TV Week The RFDS crew: Rodney Afif, Ash Ricardo, Emma Harvie, Rob Collins, Emma Hamilton, Sofia Nolan and Jack Scott. Getty Images



Monica O’Brien and Lisa Millar accept the award. Getty Images for TV Week “Telling regional Australian stories is incredibly important,” the actor who plays Dr Eliza Harrod said backstage. “Australia is a vast country, and a lot of the stories that get told on screen are centred on the coast. It’s beautiful to be able to reveal the spectacular landscape and the beating heart of this country, both with rural communities and First Nations communities, and everyone who makes up the fabric of the vast majority of this country. “It is a privilege and an honour to bring those stories to life. I feel like I’ve grown as a person telling those stories, and I’m sure I’m not alone.” Related Article Exclusive

Logies ‘It would be churlish to say no’: Why this TV legend had mixed feelings about the Logies Hall of Fame Lisa Millar expressed similar sentiments after Muster Dogs won for best structured reality program.

Her duties as host of that show and Backroads, both for the ABC, meant she was on the road in rural and regional Australia for 125 days a year. “It’s really lovely to get out of the cities and rediscover how people feel about the ABC and feel about the programs,” she said.



Muster Dogs resonated, she suggested, because it’s a bit of an antidote to the grimness of the news. “It’s something people can switch on with their families and sit there with their kids. It makes them feel happy, it lifts their spirits, and I am so grateful that I get to be a part of that.” With A Country Practice also being inducted into the Hall of Fame, the cynical might observe that the focus on the regions might have owed something to the fact Logies host Seven is particularly strong in those markets. But this didn’t really feel like a night for cynicism. “I just want to spend as much time as I can pumping positivity out in the world,” said Irwin backstage after winning the award for most popular presenter. Robert Irwin poses with the Bert Newton Award for most popular presenter for I’m A Celebrity … Get Me Out Of Here! Getty Images Even Pang, whose biting humour had been a highlight of the past three years, was won over. “He’s doing a wonderful job,” he said when asked if he had any notes for the new kid. “It’s different, obviously, to the ones I did, but he’s just talented and wonderful and we’re all enjoying it.”



For all the warm glow, there was an inescapable sadness about the night, too. The passing of Sam Neill last month and of Johnny Young last week both landed hard, and the In Memoriam segment jolted with reminders of others gone in the past year: James Valentine, Mel Schilling, Derryn Hinch, David Stratton, John Laws, Rhoda Roberts, Terence Donovan and so many more. Even there, though, there was a note of optimism to be found in the words of Neill, as relayed by his longtime friend Heather Mitchell. “He took every opportunity to open his heart and share his life and his talent with all of us. He gave us courage and hope, and very fine wine,” said Mitchell. “To quote Sam: ‘I know it’s easy to spiral down and think what’s the worst thing that can happen, but I encourage you to spiral up and think what’s the best thing that can happen. Look up. It’s blue.’”

World.title: Haddara crime family boss shot in Altona North
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaCrime Haddara crime family boss shot in Altona North Chris Vedelago and Roy Ward Updated August 17, 2026 — 12:56am ,first published 10:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police are investigating after a man believed to be the alleged one-time gangland boss Fadi Haddara was shot in Altona North this evening. Haddara’s lawyer has been contacted for comment. Fadi Haddara Jason South The Age has heard from multiple sources that Haddara was shot while parked in a car in his driveway on Marigold Avenue near Millers Road and is receiving treatment at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. He is believed to be in a stable condition.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime When the head of a crime family found trackers on his car, he knew the game was up Haddara, alleged patriarch of the Haddara crime family, once held a commanding position over the illicit tobacco trade in Melbourne but had been squeezed out by new gangland boss Kazem “Kaz” Hamad in early 2024. Police said a 48-year-old man was shot and later taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries in what they believe, at this stage, was a targeted attack. The Age has previously reported that the Haddaras surrendered their stake in the illicit tobacco smuggling and distribution market following a relentless firebombing and shooting campaign waged by Hamad in 2023-2024, including Fadi finding multiple GPS trackers on his car. The attack on Fadi has been met with surprise in the underworld given the clan was largely sidelined following Hamad’s establishment of cartel-like control over the tobacco market.



Attempts by some criminal players to take advantage of Hamad’s arrest in Iraq in January have met with acts of serious retribution by Hamad’s gang, known as The Commission or the 313. From left: Waleed Haddara, Fadi Haddara, Sam Abdulrahim and his trainer Pierre Karam. Instagram Four businesses and a home owned or linked to the crime gang led by Haddara were attacked in March of this year alone, including the torching of the Capriccio Gelateria in Williamstown and a drive-by shooting targeting a crowd of men standing outside an Altona North kebab shop in the heart of the gang’s territory. Emergency services were at the house on Sunday night where Haddara was shot with Armed Crime Squad detectives investigating and the major crime scene unit set to attend the scene early on Monday. World.title: Limericks, sandwiches and a trip to Antarctica: Sam Neill’s friends pay tribute at moving Logies
World.content:
CultureTV & radioLogies Limericks, sandwiches and a trip to Antarctica: Sam Neill’s friends pay tribute at moving Logies Karl Quinn August 17, 2026 — 12:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This year’s Logies ceremony was always going to be about Sam Neill to some extent. But a win in the best actor category for his role as barrister Brett Colby in The Twelve afforded a double opportunity to celebrate the career of the much-loved New Zealander, who died from pneumonia at the age of 78 last month. Johnny Young’s death last week would probably have thrown planning for the In Memoriam segment into disarray had it been anyone other than Neill at the top of everyone’s list of TV people we will miss. Katie Noonan’s performance of Crowded House’s Don’t Dream It’s Over, a favourite of the Jurassic Park star, was not to be displaced, though, no matter how strong the lure of the Beatles’ All My Loving (the signature tune of Young Talent Time) might have been. Loading On the red carpet, Heather Mitchell, who was nominated for best supporting actress for The Narrow Road to the Deep North, said Neill, a longtime friend and a frequent collaborator – including in the forthcoming feature The Fox – is already “greatly, greatly, greatly missed”. She shared a couple of memories of her friend, the first personal. “I was very fortunate that my husband and I went on a trip with Sam a couple of years ago to the sub-Antarctic, and we followed the albatross,” she said. “That will always be a very, very fond memory for me.”



Editor's pick Logies Logies 2026 as it happened: Sam Pang wins Gold Logie; touching tributes to Sam Neill and Johnny Young; Deborah Mailman inducted into Hall of Fame The other was professional. Though exactly how professional is perhaps open to debate. “He directed me once in a series and I had to bark like a dog while I was having sex,” said Mitchell. “And I remember him doing it for me.” And with that she joyously recreated the moment, with some of the wildest woofing the Logies red carpet has ever witnessed. On stage, Mitchell had the double duty of speaking about Neill during the In Memoriam segment and again as she accepted his acting award. “I’m so sorry I’m not Sam,” she said on the latter occasion. “I know how much this would mean to Sam ... this is an indication of his connection, the connection he has with people, with his audience.”



Danielle Cormack worked with her fellow Kiwi (to be fair, a term Neill bristled at) on the third season of The Twelve: Cape Rock Killer. “I literally sat with him for months because we were in court together,” she said, confiding that to while away the downtime between set-ups, “we started a limerick competition. I was going through some of my admin the other day and I came across some of the limericks he’d written for me.” Katie Noonan onstage during the In Memorium segment honouring Sam Neill at the Logie Awards on Sunday night. Getty Images for TV Week Any family-friendly enough to share? “It was a lot to do with actors and actresses – none mentioning bishops – but a lot to do with out-of-work actresses,” she said, laughing. “I don’t know what he was hinting at.” Simon Baker, who won the best supporting actor award for The Narrow Road to the Deep North, said Neill was “dignified and beautiful and had great poise. He was very generous towards me, very kind and warm and funny and caring. He was dignity.”



Heather Mitchell speaks about her late friend Sam Neill on stage at the Logies. Getty Images for TV Week Claudia Karvan – another winner, as best supporting actor for Homebodies – last saw Neill just a month before he died. “He was just desperate to get back to work,” she said. Though he was a bona fide international star, there were no airs and graces about Neill, said Karvan, who recalled working with him on The House of Hancock, a show she produced. She recalled being out in the desert, the cast and crew sharing dongas, the catering consisting of a table set up with bread and butter and instructions to make your own sandwiches. “And I was like, ‘Oh no, he’s gonna call his agent and get choppered out of here’. But he just queued up and made his own sandwiches like everyone else.” Leigh Sales, host of the ABC’s The Assembly, which won the Logie for best factual or documentary program, said it was “poignant” to revisit Neill’s screen roles in light of his recent passing. And given Neill was the first guest on The Assembly, in which a group of autistic journalism students interview celebrities, that includes her own program. “To see bits of that again [was to be] reminded of how terrific he was on screen,” she said. “I think the way he came across in his social media, when he was on his farm, that’s really how he came across [in life], Sales said. “A real gentleman.”

World.title: Sam Pang takes home Gold as Robert Irwin shines: Full list of winners at the 2026 Logie Awards
World.content:
Sam Pang may have handed the reins over to Robert Irwin for the 66th TV Week Logie Awards, but those watching at home clearly missed the former host up on The Star stage. First was Have You Been Paying Attention?’s best comedy entertainment program victory, which was one of three Logies taken home by Network 10 tonight. Well, four counting Pang’s Gold Logie victory, which, technically, also added to Seven (The Front Bar) and the ABC’s (Ground Up) tallies – no wonder he’s the most popular person on Australian television. But how does he feel about that honour? First nomination, first victory: Sam Pang is officially the most popular personality on Australian television after winning the Gold Logie. Getty Images for TV Week “It’s been a weird life, like all I wanted to do was I just try to be funny,” Pang said backstage after joking with the media that it’s not his family he celebrates with first – it’s the press pack lying in wait. “It’s just very, very weird... I grew up watching the Logies... I never thought I was gonna be on television, let alone win anything, like Have You Been Paying Attention? won a Logie, and now to win gold. I’m lost for words.”







Pang may have taken home the gold, but Irwin – who did win Bert Newton award for most popular presenter – was also a big winner of the night. He did, after all, succeed at what was seemingly an impossible mission: to make free-to-air cool enough for the TikTok generation to tune in.
